metadata.title: The Harvest
metadata.description: You wake in a stasis pod aboard a massive alien vessel. The Choir — eyeless bio-mechanical drones — are harvesters serving an ancient intelligence called The Convergence that consumes planets. Your pod malfunctioned. You're loose on a ship full of things that want you back in the jar. Below, a planet is being consumed alive.
metadata.author: ai-generated

setting.ambient_text: A subsonic hum vibrates through your bones. Amber fluid drains from your cracked pod, pooling on the organic-metallic floor. Bioluminescent veins pulse in the walls. Somewhere, something clicks — precise, mechanical, patient.
intro_text:
You remember fragments.
A world with... two suns? Or was it one?. Fields of amber grain.
Faces you can no longer name.

Then the sky split open.
Something vast descended — a living ship,
all tendrils and bioluminescent veins.
It took everything.

You were catalogued.
Weighed. Measured. Filed away in a pod
of warm amber fluid alongside
hundreds of other specimens.

You don't know how long you slept.
Days. Months. Years.
The ship hums around you —
a heartbeat that is not your own.

Something has gone wrong.
Your pod is cracked. The fluid is draining.
Alarms pulse in colors you have no name for.
The ship's crew is nowhere to be seen.

You are cold. You are weak.
You are alone on a vessel
built to harvest worlds.

Find a way out.

hints.text: Your stasis pod is shattered. Search the wreckage — the broken glass and pooling fluid might be useful.
Your broken pod is a source of useful materials. Search it thoroughly before moving on.

The amber fluid pooling beneath the drainage channel could be useful, but you need a container. There must be other rooms on this ship — one of them might have something you could use — sample jars, perhaps.
You have a sample jar. Use it on the drainage channel to collect some of that amber stasis fluid.
There's a specimen tag on a hook nearby — it has your identification on it. Take it.
You've gathered what you can here. The cataloguer robot on the wall might be worth investigating, and the archway leads deeper into the ship.
Study the three specimens — a Velith Ammonite, a Kethrani Weaver, and a Neural Orchid. The display screens below each tank show numbers alongside the alien text.
You've already noted the section code: 7-3-1-9. The terminal keypad in the processing lab might accept it.
The terminal has alien keypads. If you had an access code, you might be able to enter it here.
You know the code 7-3-1-9 from the specimen data plates. Try entering it on the keypad.
You've unlocked the terminal. Check all the readouts — there might be more to learn.
A specimen processing lab. The surgical instruments and data screens might be worth investigating.
The instrument rack holds alien surgical tools. Take one — it could serve as a makeshift tool. The sample jars on the shelf might also have something useful.
One of the sample jars on the lower shelf looks empty and cracked open. You could use it to collect liquids.
The lab data screens are still active. Look at them closely — they might contain security codes or ship layout data.
You've found a security access sequence in the lab data. Head to the security hub in the corridor to use it.
Look at the lab data screens again for a closer view of the terminal. If you have a section code, you might be able to unlock restricted data.
You've unlocked the lab terminal and discovered the Convergence's harvesting route. Continue exploring the ship.
This corridor connects the containment sections. Explore the passages branching off in each direction.
The passage to the left might have tools and information. The passage to the right could give you control over the ship's systems.
You've accessed security. The passage straight ahead leads deeper into the ship and connects to more areas worth exploring.
You know this corridor well now. Make sure you've explored every branch before looking for a way off this deck.
The security override released the ventilation grate in the floor. It leads deeper into the ship — toward the airlock bay.
A grim place. The ship's crew dispose of failed specimens here. Search the room — even in death, there may be something useful.
A severed neural tendril lies near one of the slabs. Alien neural tissue could have applications elsewhere.
You've taken the neural tendril. The recycling vats and drawers tell a grim story, but you've found what's useful here.
The feeding station connects to the morgue, the specimen archive, and the corridor. Explore the passages leading left and right.
The nutrient dispenser still functions. The paste isn't appetizing, but it might have other uses.
The morgue is through the left passage, and the specimen archive is to the right. Both may hold items you need.
Make sure you've explored the morgue and the archive thoroughly. The airlock bay beyond the ventilation shaft is your way off this deck.
The scratches on the walls look deliberate. Maybe you should examine them more closely.
Your map shows the way through the maze ahead. The left path at the junction is marked as correct.
The ventilation shaft branches ahead. This was someone else's escape route before yours.
The wall markings might mean something. Too bad you don't have a reference.
Your map says LEFT is the way. The helmet symbol means you'll need protection.
Two paths. One is correct. The air currents might give you a clue.

views.name: Gas-Filled Passage
views.ambient_text: Yellow-green gas swirls around you. Every breath burns.

hints.text: The gas is lethal without protection. You need something to breathe through safely.
The helmet should protect you from the gas. Press forward.
This section is filled with toxic gas from a cracked bio-organic pipe.
The fan's mechanism has an exposed gap, but you don't have anything to jam it with. Did you leave a tool behind?
The fan mechanism has an exposed gap. Something long and thin — like your surgical probe — might jam the gears.
The fan is stopped. You can squeeze through the blades now.
A massive fan blocks the passage. Its mechanism is exposed on the wall.
The skeleton is holding something. It still glows faintly.
A dead end, but not a wasted trip. The skeleton tells a story.
The skeleton had more than just a datapad. Search the body again — check their uniform pockets.
The airlock bay is below. Drop through the hatch to reach it.
The security console is dark. You need an access sequence to activate it — perhaps the processing lab has one.
You know the access sequence from the lab. Use it on the security console to bring the system online.
The console is active. Try overriding the containment locks to open more of the ship. Also check the drawer for useful items.
You have the key card and the locks are overridden. The rest of the containment deck should be accessible now.
The security console needs a code to activate. Have you checked the specimen data plates in the stasis hold?
You know the code is 7-3-1-9 from the data plates. Try entering it on the keypad.
The console is active. Check the override lever — it controls the containment locks for the entire deck.
All locks are overridden. Don't forget the key card in the drawer — and check the surveillance feeds.
The archive holds records of every species the Choir have collected. The data crystals and reading device could reveal vital information.
One of the data crystals is out of place — a personal log, perhaps. Take it and use the reading device to access its contents.
You have the data crystal. Insert it into the reading device to decrypt its contents.
The holographic display shows the Convergence's path of destruction across galaxies. Examine it to understand what you're up against.
You've uncovered the Choir's records and the Convergence's history. This knowledge will be crucial as you go deeper.
An airlock bay. Your ship might have been docked here. Look around for supplies and a way to open the outer doors.
The docking clamps are empty — your ship is gone. Check the suit locker and the viewport.
The suit locker might contain an emergency helmet. Open it and take what you can.
The manual override panel is locked tight. You'll need a containment key card — the security hub might have one.
You have the containment key card. Use it on the override panel to unlock the airlock systems.
The bridge holds the ship's star charts and navigation systems. Understanding where this vessel has been could reveal where it's going.
The star map shows the Convergence's path. The command console may have a removable navigation chip with jump coordinates.
You have the navigation data. Engineering and the comm array are accessible from here.
The ship's reactor pulses like a living heart. Look for portable power sources and coolant — both could be invaluable.
The reactor access panel might yield a power cell. The coolant system could provide a useful chemical agent.
You've salvaged what you can from engineering. The shuttle bay and waste processing are accessible from here.
The communications array handles all signals to and from The Convergence. The schematics and recording station may hold useful intelligence.
Look for the comm array schematics — understanding the frequencies could let you send your own transmissions later.
You have the schematics. The data core and navigation bridge are connected from here.
The Choir's weapons are biometrically locked, but something has already been removed from one rack. Search for anything you can actually use.
The resonance disruptor on the workbench might be operable. It disrupts bio-mechanical systems — extremely useful against Choir technology.
The resonance disruptor is yours. The hive quarters and shuttle bay connect from here.
The Choir's living quarters. Their resonance chamber and dormancy alcoves might hold items attuned to their biology.
The resonance chamber could contain a Choir crystal — their communication medium. A cipher fragment may be hidden in their patterns.
You've gathered what you can from the Choir's quarters. The armory, comm array, and waste processing are accessible from here.
A damaged shuttle sits in the bay. It might be your ticket off this ship — if you can repair it.
The shuttle needs fuel, power, and navigation to fly. Look for a fuel line in the supply rack, and bring a power cell and navigation chip from elsewhere.
You have what you need to start repairs. Install the fuel line, power cell, and navigation chip into the shuttle systems.
The ship's bio-garden grows alien plants. Some may have biochemical properties worth harvesting.
The harvest station has concentrated bio-extract, and the fiber plants produce incredibly strong strands. Take both.
You've harvested what you need. These materials can be combined with other items for new tools.
The ship's data core — an organic brain that stores all operational data. The interface terminal may let you access encrypted Convergence communications.
Use the interface terminal to query the organic brain. The Convergence's encrypted communications could reveal their plans for this planet.
You've accessed the data core. The comm array and hydroponics connect from here.
The ship's waste processing. Catwalks over grinding machinery. A dangerous place, but perhaps something useful was discarded here.
A disabled maintenance drone near the catwalks still has its sensory antenna intact. It could detect Choir patrol signals.
You've taken the drone antenna. Engineering and the hive quarters are accessible from here.
The observation deck offers a view of the planet below. The instruments here monitor the harvesting process.
Study the observation instruments carefully. Understanding the energy siphon network could be critical when you reach the surface.
You've studied the siphon network. The bridge and hydroponics connect from here.
You've crashed on the planet's surface. Search the wreckage for anything salvageable before moving on.
The shuttle interior may have an emergency beacon and other supplies. The wasteland stretches out beyond the crash site.
You've salvaged what you can. Head into the wasteland to find the planet's former inhabitants and their weapons.
The shuttle's interior is smashed but some systems still function. Check the dashboard, emergency kit, and personal storage.
The emergency beacon and signal flare could save your life. Take everything that isn't bolted down.
You've taken everything useful from the wreck.
The wasteland stretches in all directions. Paths lead to a siphon tower, a refugee camp, a fungal grove, and an overlook.
The siphon tower has energy crystals worth collecting. The refugee camp might have supplies and information from the former inhabitants.
The city gates lie beyond the echo field near the refugee camp. You'll need to prepare before venturing there.
A massive energy siphon tower drains life from the planet. The crystals at its base pulse with raw Convergence energy.
Break off a siphon crystal fragment and take a mineral sample. Both contain Convergence energy that could be weaponized.
You've collected what you need from the tower. These materials can be combined with items from the ship.
The remains of a refugee camp. The former inhabitants fled here before the end. Search their belongings for supplies and information.
A journal among the scattered belongings could contain a cipher fragment. The supply crate may still have rations and climbing gear.
You've gathered what the refugees left behind. The echo field beyond could lead to the city.
Bioluminescent fungi thrive here, feeding on the Convergence's residual energy. Their biochemistry could be potent.
Extract the concentrated fungal compounds. They could be combined with other chemicals for powerful effects.
You have the extract. A buried military bunker is accessible deeper in the grove.
Reality warps here — echoes of the dead civilization manifest as ghostly apparitions. Navigate carefully.
The echo stabilizer from the bunker could help you pass through safely. Without it, the echo field is dangerous and disorienting.
The city gates are visible through the distortion. Press on toward the dead civilization's last stronghold.
A military bunker from the planet's final days. The door may require a code. Search for one among the refugee camp's belongings.
The bunker holds military equipment — an echo stabilizer, weapons, defense schematics, and a radiation badge. Take everything.
You've taken everything useful from the bunker. The echo stabilizer will help you navigate the echo field toward the city.
The gates of the dead city loom before you. They may need a keystone or a specific approach to open.
The gates are open. The dead city awaits. The overlook nearby offers a panoramic view of what lies ahead.
From this vantage point you can see the dead city spread below, the siphon towers draining it, and the nexus at its heart.
The panoramic vista reveals the layout of the city. Study it — knowledge of the terrain will help you navigate below.
The grand plaza of a dead civilization. Explore the buildings, monuments, and pathways branching from here.
The central statue may hold a keystone — an access token for restricted areas. The map kiosk could reveal the city's layout.
You have the keystone and know the layout. The library, war room, and research lab hold the information you need to find the weapon.
The city's library — a vast collection of crystalline knowledge. The translation cipher will help you read the ancient texts.
Search the crystal stacks for the final cipher fragment. The reading station and holographic index can help decipher the planet's history.
With the cipher fragments, you can assemble a complete translation. Use it to read the Convergence section for weapon intelligence.
The military command center. The holographic table and tactical displays show the civilization's last stand against the Convergence.
The defense grid controller on the tactical table could control orbital defense satellites — if any still function.
You have the controller. The battle plans mention a countermeasure weapon — its schematics may be in the research lab.
The research lab where the countermeasure weapon was designed. The prototype and schematics are here.
Study the prototype weapon and find the assembly blueprint. You'll need to understand exactly how to build the countermeasure.
You have the blueprint and know the weapon design. The lab goggles will protect you from dangerous energy when you reach the nexus.
Homes abandoned in haste. The packed luggage and half-eaten meals paint a picture of sudden evacuation.
A personal locket among the possessions might hold emotional significance. An echo of a former resident may appear if you're still enough.
You've seen the lives that were lived here. Their memory drives you forward.
The city's power station. The reactor is offline but the backup systems might be restorable.
Restart the reactor to power the city's systems. The power distribution panel and adapter will let you bridge alien technology together.
Power is restored. The city's transit system and other infrastructure should be functional now.
A sacred place. The resonance chamber and altar held spiritual significance for the former inhabitants.
The prophet's crystal on the altar shows visions of possible futures. The resonance tuning fork could communicate with echoes.
You have the crystal and tuning fork. These sacred tools may prove decisive at the nexus.
The city's underground transit. The rails lead deeper — toward the weapon vault and the nexus beyond.
The railway controls need a pass token and power to function. Check the platform area for a token.
You have the pass token. With city power restored, the railway can take you deeper.
Reality splits here — one half pristine, one half ruined. A ghost scientist lingers at the boundary.
The echo communicator could let you speak with the ghost scientist. They may know the vault's access codes.
The scientist's echo has shared what it knows. The weapon vault should be accessible now.
The weapon vault — where the countermeasure was stored. Security systems still guard the weapon core.
The biometric lock requires ancient access authorization. The vault's energy barriers and security door must be bypassed.
The weapon core sits on its pedestal. Take it — this is what the entire civilization built to fight the Convergence.
The ground crystallizes beneath your feet. The nexus is close — reality itself bends around the Convergence's power.
Press forward. The entrance to the nexus lies ahead. Prepare everything you have — there may be no turning back.
The nexus gate pulses with Convergence energy. Ancient markings from the former inhabitants surround the entrance.
Study the ancient markings — they may reveal how the former civilization intended to approach the nexus. The descent tunnel leads down.
Rivers of raw energy flow through massive conduits. A narrow metal walkway spans the chasm.
The shielded helmet will protect you from the energy. Cross the walkway to reach the convergence chamber. An energy sample point could yield pure Convergence energy.
The heart of the harvesting apparatus. A beam of energy connects the planet's core to the ship above. This is where it all ends — or begins.
The countermeasure slot at the base of the apparatus is where the weapon must be deployed. Assemble the countermeasure from the weapon core and your gathered components.
The assembled countermeasure is ready. Place it in the slot to end the harvesting — but consider your options. There may be other ways to resolve this.
The control spire oversees the entire harvesting operation. Choir consoles and ancient controls coexist here.
The spire interface module could let you communicate directly with the Convergence. The ancient controls might offer alternative solutions.
A gallery of the Convergence's oldest specimens — civilizations consumed across eons. A pedestal holds an ancient access key.
Take the ancient access key from the pedestal. It opens the deepest sections of the nexus.
A staging area where the former inhabitants prepared their assault on the nexus. The workbench can assemble complex devices.
Use the assembly workbench to combine the weapon core with your gathered components. The blueprint shows the full recipe.
The countermeasure is assembled. Take it to the convergence chamber to deploy it.
A crystal antenna array capable of broadcasting across the galaxy. The consoles control targeting and frequency.
With the comm schematics and a galactic broadcast assembled, you could warn other civilizations about the Convergence.
The Convergence itself. An ancient intelligence, vast and patient, that has consumed worlds for longer than most stars have burned.
The core interface point allows direct neural contact with the Convergence. You could confront it, reason with it, or merge with it. Choose carefully — this decides everything.
A vertical shaft carved by the former inhabitants as an emergency exit. It leads to the surface — and freedom, if you can reach it.
The shaft gate requires a key. The carved ladder leads up, but a collapsed section blocks the way. The climbing pitons could help.
The shaft is open. Climb toward the light above — but are you sure you've done everything you needed to?

items.name: Empty Sample Jar
items.description: A small bio-organic jar from the processing lab. Sealed once, now empty. Perfect for collecting liquid samples.

then.text: A small cylindrical jar made from the same bio-organic material as everything else on this ship. The seal is broken but the jar itself is intact. It could hold a few ounces of liquid.
The jar is lighter than glass and slightly warm. The interior still smells faintly of formaldehyde — or whatever alien equivalent preserved its previous contents.

items.name: Stasis Fluid Vial
items.description: A vial of amber stasis fluid from your broken pod. The liquid shimmers faintly, still biologically active.

then.text: The fluid is warm and viscous, with a faint amber glow. It preserved you — and hundreds of other specimens — in suspended animation. The biochemistry is alien but clearly designed to sustain organic life.
You swirl the vial gently. The fluid moves like honey, clinging to the glass. Something about it feels... alive.

items.name: Pod Glass Shard
items.description: A curved shard from your broken stasis pod. Sharp enough to cut.

then.text: Translucent and curved, still faintly stained with amber fluid. The edges are razor-sharp. Not glass exactly — some alien composite that's stronger and lighter.
You test the edge against your thumb. It draws blood immediately. Careful with this.

items.name: Surgical Probe
items.description: An alien surgical instrument — curved bone-like material with a fine tip.

then.text: It looks grown rather than manufactured — smooth bone-like material tapering to a needle-fine point. The handle has organic ridges shaped for fingers much longer than yours. But it fits well enough in your small hands.

items.name: Containment Key Card
items.description: A bio-organic access card pulled from the security hub. Pulses faintly with stored energy.

then.text: Not plastic — something closer to compressed cartilage, embedded with bioluminescent circuits. It pulses like a heartbeat. Keyed to the containment deck's security systems.

items.name: Data Crystal — Personal Log
items.description: A small crystalline data storage device from the specimen archive. Contains a Choir officer's personal records.

then.text: The crystal is the size of your thumb, faceted, with internal light patterns that shift when you tilt it. A Choir personal log — and embedded in the data structure, fragments of a translation cipher. This is piece one of four.

items.name: Nutrient Paste Tube
items.description: A tube of grey nutrient slurry from the feeding station. Smells like wet cardboard and ozone.

then.text: Standard specimen feed. The tube is soft, organic material. The paste inside is grey, odorless, nutritionally complete for a dozen different species. Edible but unappetizing. Could also be used as bait — the drones are programmed to retrieve spilled feed.

items.name: Specimen Tag
items.description: Your own specimen identification tag from the stasis pod. Proof of what you are to them.

then.text: A small organic tag, pulled from your pod's label slot. Alien script — you can't read it yet — but it's your entry in their collection. Proof that you were catalogued. Proof that you exist as something more than a specimen.

items.name: Emergency Suit Helmet
items.description: An alien emergency space helmet. Too large for you, but still functional.

then.text: Designed for a Choir skull — far too large for you, but the visor seals automatically when worn. The internal atmosphere system still works. It would protect you from vacuum or toxic environments, even if it sits like a fishbowl on your shoulders.

items.name: Ventilation Map
items.description: Scratches in the vent shaft walls that form a crude map. You traced them onto a flat surface.

then.text: Someone — or something — scratched a map of the ventilation system into the shaft walls. Previous escape attempts. The map shows branching paths between containment sections, and marks dead ends with deep gouges. One path leads to the operational decks.

items.name: Severed Neural Tendril
items.description: A section of neural interface tendril, severed from a alien dormancy alcove.

then.text: Rubbery, organic, about a foot long. The cut end still sparks faintly with bio-electric impulses. The Choir use these to interface with their ship's systems. With the right adapter, you could too — if you could trick it into accepting non-Choir biology.

items.name: Ship's Black Box
items.description: The Choir vessel's flight recorder. Contains the complete mission log — including records of every world consumed.

then.text: A dense, heavily shielded data device. It contains everything: navigation logs, mission parameters, specimen records, and communications with The Convergence. This is proof of what they've done — and what they're doing to the planet below.

items.name: Power Cell
items.description: A Choir power cell from engineering. Compact, immensely powerful, warm to the touch.

then.text: Bio-organic casing around a dense energy core. It hums faintly and radiates warmth. A single cell powers a Choir shuttle for weeks. Handle with care — damage to the casing would release the stored energy violently.

items.name: Resonance Disruptor
items.description: A Choir tool repurposed as a weapon. Emits a subsonic pulse that disrupts bio-mechanical systems.

then.text: Not a weapon by design — it's a maintenance tool for recalibrating Choir mechanisms. But aimed at a bio-organic lock, it scrambles the resonance patterns. Aimed at a drone, it disrupts motor functions for a few seconds. In your hands, it's the closest thing to a universal key.

items.name: Navigation Chip
items.description: A crystalline navigation module from the bridge. Contains star charts and jump coordinates.

then.text: A slim crystal wafer etched with navigation data. Star charts, jump coordinates, the Convergence's mapped path across galaxies. Without this, no ship leaves this system — the jump points are too complex to calculate manually.

items.name: Translation Cipher Fragment 2
items.description: A data pattern extracted from the Choir's resonance chamber. The second piece of the translation key.

then.text: Extracted from the communal resonance patterns in the Choir's living quarters. Their 'language' is subsonic vibration, and this fragment maps vibration patterns to meaning. Combined with the other fragments, it could let you read all alien text.

items.name: Choir Resonance Crystal
items.description: A crystal from the ship's data core that resonates at the Choir's communication frequency.

then.text: Deep purple, perfectly smooth, vibrating at a frequency you can feel in your teeth. It's tuned to the Choir's subsonic communication band — a piece of their network made solid. The same resonance frequency the Convergence uses to control its harvesters.

items.name: Bio-Garden Extract
items.description: A concentrated extract from the ship's hydroponics bay. Bioluminescent, biochemically complex.

then.text: Harvested from the alien plants in the bio-garden. The extract glows faintly blue-green and contains an extraordinary density of biological compounds. The Choir uses it for everything from nutrition to neural repair. In the right combination, it could interface organic with crystalline systems.

items.name: Comm Array Schematics
items.description: Technical diagrams of the ship's communication array. Details frequencies, power requirements, and range.

then.text: Detailed schematics showing the communications array's architecture. Frequency ranges, power routing, targeting systems. With these, the array on the planet's nexus could be recalibrated to broadcast across the galaxy — if you could reach it.

items.name: Shuttle Fuel Line
items.description: A replacement fuel conduit for the damaged shuttle. Organic tubing with self-sealing connectors.

then.text: Bio-organic tubing that carries fuel from the bay's supply to the shuttle's engines. The connectors seal automatically when pressed into place. You'll need this, plus a power cell, to get the damaged shuttle flight-ready.

items.name: Drone Antenna
items.description: A sensory antenna pulled from a disabled maintenance drone. Still picks up Choir signals.

then.text: A thin, segmented antenna that twitches faintly in your hand — it's still receiving signals. It picks up the subsonic frequencies the Choir use to coordinate. Holding it near your ear, you can hear distant clicks and hums. An early warning system.

items.name: Coolant Flask
items.description: A sealed flask of reactor coolant from engineering. Extremely cold, mildly corrosive.

then.text: The flask is frosted on the outside — the coolant inside is near absolute zero. A crack in the seal would release a burst of freezing vapor. Useful for cooling overheated systems, or as an emergency weapon against anything organic.

items.name: Bio-Garden Fiber
items.description: Strong, flexible fiber harvested from alien plants. Tougher than any natural rope.

then.text: Harvested from the tendrils of the hydroponics plants. Incredibly strong and flexible — the Choir use it in construction and repair. It can be woven, tied, or wrapped. Combined with something sharp, it would make an excellent handle or binding.

items.name: Shuttle Emergency Beacon
items.description: A distress beacon from the crashed shuttle. Can recall any shuttle within signal range.

then.text: A compact transmitter designed to recall a shuttle to its beacon location. The signal range covers the entire planet. If there's a working shuttle in orbit or on the surface, this will bring it to you. Your ticket off this rock — if you choose to leave.

items.name: Wasteland Mineral Sample
items.description: Crystalline mineral from the base of a siphon tower. Infused with residual Convergence energy.

then.text: The soil near the siphon towers has been transformed — crystallized by the Convergence's energy extraction. This sample still holds a faint charge, a dampened echo of the energy that flows through the towers. It resists energy flow rather than conducting it.

items.name: Siphon Crystal Fragment
items.description: A fragment broken from an energy siphon tower. Pulses with raw Convergence energy.

then.text: It burns cold in your hand and crackles with contained energy. A piece of the Convergence's harvesting infrastructure, still charged with stolen planetary life force. Incredibly dangerous. Incredibly powerful. A key component for anything that needs to interact with Convergence energy systems.

items.name: Refugee Journal
items.description: A personal journal from the refugee camp. Written by a four-armed scientist in the final days.

then.text: The journal of Dr. Kaelith, a physicist who fled the city when the siphons began. Entries detail the final days — the panic, the failed defenses, the evacuation that came too late. Embedded in the margins: notation patterns that match the translation cipher format. Fragment three of four.

items.name: Fungal Extract
items.description: A concentrated extract from the bioluminescent fungi in the grove. Glows purple in the dark.

then.text: The fungi survived the Convergence's harvesting — they feed on the residual energy rather than being drained by it. The extract has remarkable properties: it promotes healing in organic tissue and, combined with the right compounds, can suppress neural detection.

items.name: Echo Stabilizer
items.description: Military-grade alien technology from the bunker. Stabilizes the energy field around Echoes, making them safe to approach.

then.text: A handheld device that projects a stabilization field. The planet's military developed it to study the Echoes — remnants of their people trapped in the Convergence's energy. It calms the chaotic energy patterns, making Echoes coherent enough to interact with safely. Without it, getting close to an Echo is like standing in a lightning storm.

items.name: Alien Sidearm
items.description: A four-armed species' personal weapon. Energy-based, partially charged.

then.text: Designed for a four-armed grip — you need both hands to hold it steady. The energy cell is partially depleted: maybe six shots. Each shot is devastatingly loud. Use it wisely, or not at all.

items.name: Bunker Defense Schematics
items.description: Military blueprints showing the planet's defense strategy against the Convergence.

then.text: Detailed military plans for the planet's last stand. Orbital defense satellite positions, ground-based weapon emplacements, and — most importantly — partial schematics for a weapon designed to disrupt the Convergence's energy systems. The plans are incomplete, but they confirm the weapon was built.

items.name: Survival Rations
items.description: Preserved alien food from the refugee camp. Still sealed, still edible.

then.text: Vacuum-sealed packages of concentrated nutrition. The labels show a four-armed figure eating contentedly. Not designed for your biology, but close enough. Eating one restores energy and clears your head.

items.name: Signal Flare
items.description: An emergency signal flare from the crashed shuttle. Burns bright, burns loud.

then.text: A human-made signal flare from the Outrider's emergency kit. Pull the cap and it burns blinding white for thirty seconds. Useful as a signal, a light source, a distraction, or — wrapped with the right material — an improvised torch.

items.name: Climbing Pitons
items.description: Metal spikes from the refugee camp's supplies. Designed for climbing rocky terrain.

then.text: Alien-made climbing aids — hardened metal spikes with looped heads for roping. The refugees used them to navigate the wasteland's shattered terrain. Essential for vertical surfaces your small stature can't otherwise reach.

items.name: Radiation Badge
items.description: A sensor badge from the bunker. Changes color in the presence of dangerous Convergence energy.

then.text: A simple but effective device — the crystalline strip changes color from green (safe) to yellow (caution) to red (lethal). The planet's military used them to navigate near siphon towers and Convergence infrastructure. Near the nexus, it'll be essential for finding safe paths.

items.name: City Keystone
items.description: An ornamental keystone from the grand plaza's central statue. Opens restricted areas throughout the city.

then.text: A crystalline key shaped like a miniature four-armed figure. It was built into the plaza's central statue — a city administrator's master key. It interfaces with the city's door systems, granting access to government buildings, the war room, and restricted infrastructure.

items.name: Translation Cipher Fragment 4
items.description: The final fragment of the translation cipher, found in the city's library.

then.text: The library's master index contained the final cipher fragment — a Rosetta stone the city's linguists compiled to communicate with the Choir during failed negotiations. With all four fragments, you can read every piece of alien text in the game.

items.name: Weapon Core
items.description: The heart of the civilization's countermeasure weapon. A dense crystalline sphere pulsing with contained energy.

then.text: Heavy for its size — it feels like holding a small star. The weapon core was designed to resonate at the Convergence's own frequency, turning its stolen energy back on itself. Alone it's inert. Combined with the right components, it becomes the key to destroying the nexus.

items.name: Defense Grid Controller
items.description: A command module for the planet's orbital defense satellite network.

then.text: The planet's last line of defense — a controller for orbital weapons satellites. Most satellites are destroyed, but a few remain dormant in orbit. With enough power, they could be reactivated for one devastating strike.

items.name: Alien Personal Locket
items.description: A delicate locket from a residential home. Contains a holographic family portrait.

then.text: A small crystalline locket on a chain. Inside: a holographic portrait of a four-armed family — two adults, three children, all smiling. The youngest is holding a toy that looks like a simplified version of the siphon towers. They had no idea what was coming. Carrying this near coherent Echoes triggers powerful reactions.

items.name: Power Cell Adapter
items.description: An adapter that bridges the planet's technology with alien power sources.

then.text: The city's engineers designed this to interface their technology with captured Choir power cells. It converts between bio-organic energy formats and the civilization's crystalline power systems. A universal translator for alien technology.

items.name: Prophet's Crystal
items.description: A sacred crystal from the temple. Shows visions of possible futures when held.

then.text: The temple's priests used crystals like this for divination — and they were right more often than chance allows. Holding it, you see flashes: a nexus in flames. A signal reaching distant stars. A crystalline intelligence, afraid. A small creature, choosing. The visions are fragmented but feel profoundly real.

items.name: Railway Pass Token
items.description: An access token for the city's underground transit system.

then.text: A small crystalline disc — a transit pass. The underground railway still has power in some sections. This token activates the rail cars, allowing fast travel between the city's districts. The tunnels also connect to deeper passages beneath the city.

items.name: Resonance Tuning Fork
items.description: A ceremonial tuning fork from the temple. Vibrates at the frequency of the former civilization's communication.

then.text: The four-armed species communed through vibration, like the Choir but natural. This tuning fork produces their base resonance frequency. Combined with the Echo Stabilizer, it could enable full two-way communication with coherent Echoes — letting you truly speak with the dead.

items.name: Lab Safety Goggles
items.description: Protective eyewear from the research lab. Filters dangerous energy wavelengths.

then.text: Oversized for your face but functional. The lenses filter the blinding energy wavelengths produced by Convergence systems. The researchers wore these when studying siphon tower samples. Essential for looking directly at high-energy areas without going blind.

items.name: Ancient Blueprint
items.description: Complete assembly instructions for the countermeasure weapon. Found in the research lab.

then.text: A holographic blueprint showing the complete countermeasure weapon assembly. Three components: a primed weapon core, an energy dampener, and a siphon crystal fragment. The assembly order is critical — wrong sequence damages the core. Core first, dampener second, crystal last.

items.name: Convergence Energy Sample
items.description: Pure Convergence energy contained in a crystalline vial. Incredibly dangerous.

then.text: The vial is cold enough to burn and bright enough to read by. Inside: pure harvested planetary energy — the lifeforce of an entire world, concentrated. The crystal containment barely holds it. This is what the Convergence feeds on. This is what it's stealing.

items.name: Ancient Access Key
items.description: A key from the Convergence's stasis gallery. Opens the deepest sections of the nexus.

then.text: Not Choir-made. Not from the planet's civilization. This key predates both — it belongs to the Convergence itself, or whatever built the original nexus infrastructure. A crystalline fractal pattern that interfaces with the oldest locks in the structure.

items.name: Curator's Signal Device
items.description: The Curator's personal communication device. Can call the Choir vessel from orbit.

then.text: Taken from — or given by — the Curator itself. This device is keyed to the Curator's authority aboard the Choir vessel. It can recall the ship, issue commands to drones, and override security protocols. In friendly hands, it's a powerful ally. In desperate hands, it's a weapon.

items.name: Core Interface Module
items.description: A module from the control spire that allows direct neural interface with the Convergence intelligence.

then.text: The Choir use these to receive instructions from the Convergence. It translates crystalline energy patterns into neural signals and vice versa. It wasn't designed for non-Choir biology, but with the right biochemical preparation, it could bridge any mind to the Convergence. The question is whether you'd come back.

items.name: Escape Shaft Key
items.description: A mechanical key that opens the former civilization's emergency escape shaft in the nexus.

then.text: Found in the weapon assembly area — the former civilization's staging ground for their assault on the nexus. This key opens the emergency shaft they carved as an exit route. The shaft leads up and out, to the planet's surface. Your way out, if you choose to take it.

items.name: Charged Sidearm
items.description: A charged sidearm.

then.text: You examine the charged sidearm.

items.name: Complete Translation Cipher
items.description: A complete translation cipher.

then.text: You examine the complete translation cipher.

items.description: A countermeasure stage2.

then.text: You examine the countermeasure stage2.

then.text: You examine the echo communicator.

items.name: Galactic Broadcast
items.description: A pre-recorded galactic broadcast signal, ready for transmission.

then.text: A carefully prepared broadcast signal containing evidence of the harvest conspiracy. If transmitted, it could alert the galactic community.

items.name: Neural Bridge
items.description: A device that creates a direct neural link between minds.

then.text: An alien neural bridge device. It could establish a direct mental connection with the Nexus consciousness.

items.name: Shadow Cat Fur
items.description: A tuft of impossibly soft black fur. It shimmers faintly with an iridescent purple sheen.

then.text: A small tuft of black fur that seems to absorb light. When you tilt it, it shimmers with deep purple and violet hues. It's unnaturally soft — like holding a piece of shadow.
You roll the fur between your fingers. It's warm, almost alive. For a moment you smell something like ozone and old libraries.

items.name: Choir Crew Datapad
items.description: A Choir-make datapad recovered from a dead crew member in the vents. Still faintly glowing.

then.text: The datapad's screen shows the last entries of a Choir crew member. Their log describes the ship's systems failing, the Curator going rogue, and their desperate attempt to reach the airlock through the vents. The final entry is coordinates — the ship's last known heading before the crash — and a security override frequency for the operational decks. This could be invaluable once you reach the upper sections.

items.name: Choir Access Chip
items.description: A small crystalline security chip from a dead Choir crew member's uniform. It pulses with a faint bio-luminescent pattern — still keyed to their clearance level.

examine.response: A translucent chip the size of a thumbnail, shot through with microscopic veins of light. Choir bio-security — it reads the holder's resonance signature and broadcasts clearance to nearby locks. The dead engineer's signature is still stored. It might fool a few doors.

The chip is warm in your palm. The bioluminescent veins pulse faster when you touch it, as if it's trying to read you. It can't — you're the wrong species — but the stored clearance might still work on Choir systems.

combinations.message: You wrap the bio-fiber tightly around the base of the glass shard, creating a secure grip. The alien fiber bonds to the glass — stronger than tape, flexible as leather. A proper blade now.

You mix the nutrient paste with the stasis fluid. The combination reacts — the paste absorbs the fluid and turns a deep amber. The stasis biochemistry that kept you unconscious for days is now concentrated in a smearable compound. Touch it and sleep.

You pulse the disruptor through the key card's bio-circuits, overwriting its access restrictions. The card flares bright, then settles to a steady glow. It no longer identifies as a specific access level — it identifies as ALL access levels.

The mineral dissolves into the stasis fluid, and the mixture crystallizes into a dense gel that absorbs energy on contact. A palm-sized blob that drinks power. Near Convergence systems, it creates a local dead zone.

You channel the disruptor's pulse through the siphon crystal. The crystal amplifies it a hundredfold — the device now emits a burst capable of overloading any energy system it's aimed at. One shot. Make it count.

The fungal extract reacts with the sedative compound, producing a paste that suppresses neural signatures. Smeared on your skin, it makes you invisible to anything that detects by energy pattern — including Echoes.

You align the two cipher fragments. The data patterns interlock — half the translation key is now complete. You can read simple alien text, but complex inscriptions still elude you. Two more fragments to go.
The refugee journal's margin notations complete a third of the cipher. The translation is becoming clearer — you can now read most operational text. One fragment remains.

The final fragment locks into place. The complete cipher unfolds in your mind like a language you always knew but forgot. Every alien inscription, every label, every record — readable. The universe just opened up.

You press the Choir crystal against the weapon core. The resonance frequency syncs — the core begins to hum, vibrating at the Convergence's own frequency. It's alive now, tuned to destroy the thing it was made to fight. Partially assembled. It needs a dampener and a power source.

The adapter accepts the navigation chip's crystalline format and bridges it to a universal power bus. The result is a device that can interface with any alien technology — Choir, Convergence, or the former civilization's systems. A skeleton key for machines.

You wire the overcharge device into the defense grid controller. The orbital satellites now have a targeting solution — and enough power for one devastating strike. Point it at the nexus and fire. Point it at the Choir ship and fire. Either way, everything changes.

You wrap the bio-fiber around the flare's head, creating a longer-burning light source. The alien fiber catches fire slowly and burns steady instead of blinding. A proper torch that'll last much longer than the flare alone.

You line the helmet's interior with the energy dampener gel. The dampener absorbs the worst of the Convergence's ambient radiation. Wearing this, you can survive the nexus's high-energy chambers without your nervous system frying.

You mount the tuning fork in the stabilizer's emitter array. The combined device doesn't just calm Echoes — it speaks their language. The stabilization field now carries your words as resonance patterns the dead can hear. And their responses come back clear.

The Choir power cell slots into the alien weapon's depleted energy chamber. The sidearm hums to life — fully charged now. Twenty shots instead of six. The four-armed grip is awkward, but the firepower is undeniable.

The energy dampener wraps around the primed core, containing its resonance while focusing its destructive potential. One more component — the siphon crystal fragment — and the countermeasure is complete.

The siphon crystal fragment snaps into the dampener housing like it was always meant to be there. The complete countermeasure weapon activates — a sphere of crystallized destruction, humming with the Convergence's own stolen energy turned against it. This kills planets. This saves them too.

objects.name: Shadow Cat
objects.description: A small black cat with glowing purple-amber eyes. It shouldn't be here. Nothing like this should exist on an alien harvester ship.

interactions.response: A black cat sits perfectly still, watching you with luminous purple-amber eyes. Its fur shimmers faintly, as if dusted with starlight. How did it get here?
You whisper to the cat. It blinks slowly — once, twice — then tilts its head as if considering whether you're worth its time.

then.text: You reach out carefully. The cat allows a single stroke along its back, then slips away into the shadows like smoke. A tuft of dark fur clings to your fingers.

interactions.response: The cat is gone. Only the memory of its strange, knowing eyes remains.
The cat watches you approach, then vanishes into the shadows before you get close.

objects.name: Your Broken Pod
objects.description: The stasis pod you woke in. The glass is cracked, amber fluid pooling beneath it. Fragments of the pod casing litter the floor.

then.text: The pod hangs open, drained of fluid. Your outline is still visible in the residue on the back wall — a small creature's impression in amber. A specimen tag dangles from the pod's frame.
You carefully snap off a curved shard of pod glass from the broken edge. It's razor-sharp — some alien composite that's stronger and lighter than real glass. A crude tool, but a tool nonetheless.
You whisper to yourself, staring at the empty pod. "How long was I in there?" The ship offers no answer, only the wet drip of stasis fluid.
The pod is fused to the wall by thick organic brackets. It's not going anywhere — and neither is what happened inside it.

objects.name: Drainage Channel
objects.description: A channel beneath the pods where spilled stasis fluid collects before being recycled.

then.text: A shallow channel cut into the floor, feeding into the ship's recycling systems. Amber stasis fluid pools here, slowly draining. The fluid shimmers with faint bioluminescence.

You cup your hands and try to scoop up the amber fluid. It's warm and viscous, almost alive — but it slips through your fingers, too thick to hold bare-handed. You'd need some kind of container. The processing lab down the corridor might have something.
The channel is mostly drained now. A thin film of amber residue clings to the groove, but nothing worth collecting.

You dip the sample jar into the amber fluid. It fills quickly — the stasis compound is thick and clings to the jar's bio-organic walls like it belongs there. The jar seals itself shut with a soft click, some residual mechanism recognizing its purpose. The fluid shimmers faintly inside, still biologically active.
You listen to the fluid gurgling into the drain. It sounds almost like breathing — a rhythmic pulse synced to something deep in the ship.
The channel is carved directly into the floor, part of the ship's living architecture. You couldn't pry it loose without tools.

objects.name: Occupied Stasis Pods
objects.description: Rows of intact pods stretching into the shadows above. Most contain dead specimens. Some glow faintly — still active.

then.text: Rows of hexagonal pods stretch up into the shadows, each glowing faintly with amber fluid. Specimens from dozens of worlds — creatures frozen in stasis, catalogued and stored. Most are still, but a few pods pulse with faint signs of life. The pods are too high to reach from here.

interactions.response: You tap on the nearest pod's surface. The amber fluid inside swirls briefly. The creature within doesn't stir.

then.text: "Can you hear me?" you murmur, pressing close to a pod. The creature inside doesn't stir. Maybe that's a mercy.

objects.name: Specimen Tag
objects.description: A small tag hanging from your pod's frame, inscribed with alien notation.

then.text: A small bio-organic tag, like a leaf made of cartilage. Alien notation is etched into its surface — your classification, probably. A serial number for a specimen. It identifies you as a collected organism. It's proof you were here. Proof you existed to them.
You snap the tag free from the pod frame. It's small enough to pocket. You're not a specimen. You're a person. But this might be useful as proof — to someone, somewhere — that you were here.
You mouth the alien numerals on the tag hook. The symbols feel wrong in your throat, like a language not meant for human vocal cords.
The hook is a small nub of bio-metal protruding from the pod frame. It bends slightly but won't break off.

objects.name: Examination Tables
objects.description: Long tables with organic restraints, designed for specimens much larger than you.

then.text: Two examination tables dominate the room. The restraints are sized for creatures far larger than you — thick organic clamps that would hold something much larger than you. Drainage channels lead to floor grates. Residue stains tell stories you don't want to hear. These tables have seen a lot of use.

You climb onto the nearest table. Standing on it gives you a better view of the room — and access to the higher shelves. The restraints twitch when you touch them, sensing biomass. You step back quickly.
The tables are anchored to the floor by thick organic stalks. They're part of the ship's anatomy, not furniture.
You mutter to yourself, studying the stained surface. "Whatever they did here... they did it to a lot of us."

You place the cat hair on the examination table's analysis plate. The table hums, its organic scanners activating automatically — it's designed to process biological samples. A holographic readout appears above the surface: 'Sol-3 Felis catus. Batch 7. Status: PROCESSED.' Processed. Your cat was here. Was analyzed. Was... harvested. A cold fury builds in your chest. You carefully retrieve the hair and pocket it. This is personal now.

objects.name: Surgical Instrument Rack
objects.description: A rack of alien surgical tools — curved bone-like instruments, probes, and extractors.

then.text: Surgical instruments arranged with obsessive precision. They look grown rather than forged — smooth bone-like material, organic curves, needle-fine tips. Most are sized for hands far larger than yours: too large for you to wield. But a smaller probe near the bottom of the rack looks manageable.

You reach for the smallest instrument — a probe with a fine, flexible tip. It fits well enough in your hands. The bone-like material is warm to the touch, almost alive. It'll work as a precision tool — lock picks, screws, delicate mechanisms.
The rack is grown directly from the wall. Pulling it would be like trying to remove a rib.
You name each tool under your breath, trying to guess their purpose. None of the shapes match any surgery you've seen. That's not reassuring.

objects.name: Sample Jars
objects.description: Shelves of preserved biological samples in sealed jars.

then.text: Dozens of sealed jars containing biological samples — tissue, fluid, organs. Each is labeled with the same alien notation you've seen on the pods. Some samples are recognizable (a heart, an eye), others are abstract shapes in fluid. Your stomach turns. One jar on the lower shelf is empty — its seal cracked open, contents long since evaporated.

Dozens of sealed jars containing biological samples — tissue, fluid, organs. Each is labeled with the same alien notation you've seen on the pods. Some samples are recognizable (a heart, an eye), others are abstract shapes in fluid. Your stomach turns.

Most of the jars are sealed tight with bio-organic resin — you'd need tools to open them. But one on the lower shelf is already cracked open, its contents dried to a crust. You pry it free. The jar itself is intact. Could be useful for collecting samples.
You reach toward the jars but pull back. The contents shift when your shadow falls across them, as if reacting to your presence.
The jars are seated in recesses molded perfectly to their shape. They weren't placed here — they were grown in place.
You lean close and whisper. The pale thing in the nearest jar twitches. You step back quickly. It heard you.

objects.name: Lab Data Screens
objects.description: Screens cycling through biological data and procedural information.

then.text: The screens cycle through processing routines: intake, classification, preservation, disposal. One screen catches your eye — a startup sequence, bio-organic buttons pressed in a specific order. Five steps, specific timing. You commit the pattern to memory and lean in closer...
You lean in to study the terminal's alien keypads up close...
The display is a bioluminescent membrane stretched across an organic frame. It can't be moved any more than you could move a patch of skin.
You try speaking to the display. A symbol flickers in response — the ship might understand vocal commands, but you don't know its language. Yet.

objects.name: Main Display
objects.description: A large green screen showing a detailed alien organism diagram with alien text annotations.

then.text: The main screen shows a detailed biological diagram — some kind of spiny, multi-limbed organism rendered in green phosphor lines. Alien text runs across the top and bottom. Two smaller sub-panels on the right show anatomical cross-sections and what looks like processing data. The alien characters are unlike anything on Earth — curved, angular, almost calligraphic. The screen is locked to this default display.

The screen has changed — it now cycles through specimen processing records. You recognize some of the organism silhouettes from the stasis hold tanks. Each record shows intake data, biological classification, and... a schedule. Processing dates. Future dates. The ship is still collecting. Still processing. Still on its route. And according to this schedule, the next harvesting stop is a planet in a system with a single yellow star. Eight planets. Third from the sun. Earth. Your home. The Convergence is heading for Earth.
The processing records continue cycling. Earth is on the harvesting schedule. You need to find a way to stop this ship — or at least warn someone — before it reaches your world.
You touch the screen surface. It ripples like a membrane — warm, slightly wet. Bioluminescent. This isn't a monitor; it's a living tissue display. The alien characters swim under your fingertips.

interactions.response: You speak to the screen. The alien characters flicker slightly, but the display doesn't respond to your voice. The Choir's systems don't understand your language.

objects.name: Alien Keypad
objects.description: A small keypad with alien characters etched into bio-organic keys.

then.text: A small keypad with alien characters etched into each key — the characters match the ones you've seen on specimen data plates throughout the ship. Some keys have numerical notations beneath the alien glyphs. This keypad accepts access codes.

interactions.response: The keypad glows a steady green — access granted. The terminal is unlocked.

then.text: You press the keys matching the sequence from the specimen data plates: 7... 3... 1... 9. Each key yields like warm cartilage. The keypad flashes green — ACCESS GRANTED. The main screen flickers and begins cycling through restricted processing records. You've unlocked the terminal.

You press a few keys experimentally. The alien characters mean nothing to you — you'd need an access code to get anywhere with this. The data plates on the specimen tanks might have section codes you could use.

interactions.response: The keypad is already showing green — the terminal is unlocked. No need to enter the code again.
The keypad doesn't respond to voice. It needs physical key presses — and the right code.

objects.name: Processing Status
objects.description: A small monitor showing processing status data and system diagnostics.

then.text: A small monitor displaying what looks like a schematic — circuit pathways and node connections rendered in green. The alien characters alongside it are indecipherable. The display is locked to this diagnostic view.

With the terminal unlocked, this monitor now shows a processing queue. Specimen intake, neural mapping, bio-integration — each step listed with status indicators. Most are complete. But one entry stands out: 'XY-97-A | C44' — marked as 'INTAKE PENDING.' That's the designation on your specimen tag. You're still in the queue. Neural Integration is scheduled. They're planning to take your mind apart and catalogue it, piece by piece.

interactions.response: The monitor's surface is the same bioluminescent membrane as the main screen. Warm, slightly damp. You can't interact with it directly — the keypad controls what it displays.
You mutter at the status display. The alien characters don't change. The processing queue doesn't care about your feelings.

objects.name: Specimen Registry
objects.description: A small monitor showing specimen classification records and biological data.

then.text: Another small monitor, this one showing what looks like tabular data — rows of alien characters with numerical columns. A specimen registry of some kind, but locked behind the same access code as the main terminal.

The registry shows every species the Convergence has collected from this sector. Hundreds of entries, organized by world of origin. You find the entries for your world — 'SOL-3' — and the list is chilling. Seventeen species catalogued. Felis catus. Canis lupus familiaris. Pan troglodytes. Homo sapiens. They've been visiting Earth for a long time, taking samples. The cat in the feeding station — it's not a coincidence. It's an escaped specimen, just like you.

interactions.response: You can't interact with this display directly. The keypad controls all the terminal's screens.
"Seventeen species from Earth," you whisper. The registry scrolls on, indifferent to your horror.

then.text: You hold the specimen tag up to the registry screen. The display flickers — it reads the tag's embedded data and pulls up your full record. XY-97-A, Classification C44. Species: Homo sapiens. Origin: SOL-3. Intake: Cycle 4,891. Status: Neural Integration Pending. Notes: 'Unusual cognitive resistance. Recommend accelerated processing.' They noticed you were different. Fighting back. And they want to process you faster because of it.

objects.name: Specimen Drawers
objects.description: Walls of drawers containing failed specimens. Most are sealed. One is partially open.

then.text: Rows of drawers, floor to ceiling, each large enough to hold a body. Most are sealed. The one that's open contains something wrapped in organic membrane — humanoid in shape, roughly your size. Whatever it was, it didn't survive the collection process.

You slide the open drawer further out. The creature inside is... similar to you. Same general build, same proportions. A different species, but close enough to be unsettling. It didn't make it. You almost didn't either.
"How many of us have they processed?" you whisper. The drawers offer no answer, but the sheer number speaks volumes.
The drawers are built into the wall itself — organic metal fused seamlessly into the ship's structure.

objects.name: Autopsy Slab
objects.description: A central examination surface with drainage channels and overhead lighting.

then.text: A slab designed for dissection. Drainage channels lead to the recycling vats. Overhead, articulated lighting rigs are frozen mid-position, aimed at where a specimen's torso would be. The slab is clean — recently used and cleaned. Whoever runs this place is thorough.
The slab's surface is slick with a thin biological film. Your fingers leave trails in it. You wipe your hand on your clothes, suppressing a gag.
"I don't want to think about what happened here," you murmur. The drainage grooves in the slab tell you anyway.
The slab is anchored to the floor by thick organic cables. It's not going anywhere — and neither were its occupants.

objects.name: Recycling Vats
objects.description: Large vats where failed specimens are dissolved and their biological material reclaimed.

then.text: Three vats of viscous green liquid, bubbling slowly. The ship recycles everything — failed specimens become raw material for the bio-gardens, the hull, the instruments. Nothing is wasted. Nothing leaves.
You reach toward the vat's rim but pull back. The liquid inside bubbles faintly, and the heat radiating from it warns you away.
The vats gurgle softly, almost digestive. "They don't waste anything," you realize with growing horror.
Each vat is a deep organic basin grown directly from the floor. You couldn't move one any more than you could move a tree stump.

objects.name: Severed Neural Tendril
objects.description: A neural connection tendril, severed during whatever struggle damaged this section of the ship.

then.text: A length of neural tendril, severed from something. The cut end still pulses faintly with residual bio-electricity. This one is severed — torn during whatever struggle damaged the security hub. The cut end still pulses faintly with residual bio-electricity. It's gross. It might also be useful.

You pick up the tendril, suppressing a shudder. It's warm and slightly damp, like holding a severed worm. The bio-electricity makes your fingers tingle. The ship's technology seems to interface through things like these — plug this into the right port and you might be able to access systems keyed to their biology.
"A piece of the ship's nervous system," you think aloud. It twitches faintly, as if it heard you.
The sample is pinned to the examination surface with thin metallic spines. It squirms weakly against them.

objects.name: Nutrient Dispenser
objects.description: An automated dispenser that drips grey nutrient paste into troughs at regular intervals.

then.text: A mechanical arm dispenses grey slurry into feeding troughs on a timer. The paste smells like metal and algae. It's sustenance — barely. The dispenser connects to a central nutrient tank via transparent tubes.

You collect a tube's worth of nutrient paste from the dispenser output. It's disgusting, but grey slurry that smells like metal and algae. But you pocket a tube of it anyway. On a ship full of things that want to process you, having something foul-smelling could come in handy.
The dispenser is rooted to the wall by a tangle of feeding tubes. It pulses slightly when you push against it.
You read the dispenser's output gauge aloud. The nutrient mixture is still cycling — pale green fluid pumping through translucent tubes. Someone, or something, is still being fed.

objects.name: Feeding Troughs
objects.description: Long troughs filled with grey nutrient paste for living specimens.

then.text: Shallow troughs of grey nutrient paste, half-eaten. The paste is replenished automatically. Something has been feeding here recently — you can see marks in the paste where a creature has scooped it out.
You dip a finger into the residue lining the trough. It's thick, lukewarm, and smells faintly of copper and chlorophyll. You wipe your hand on your suit.
The troughs are carved directly into the floor — depressions in the ship's living tissue. They can't be moved.
"What were they feeding in here?" you whisper. The troughs are sized for something large — larger than you. The scrape marks along the edges suggest the occupants didn't come willingly.

objects.name: Specimen Enclosures
objects.description: Small enclosures behind shimmering energy barriers, holding living specimens.

then.text: Behind flickering energy barriers, living specimens pace in small enclosures. One enclosure holds something canine-like with too many legs. Another contains a creature that's mostly tentacles. They're alive, aware, and miserable. They watch you with recognition — another prisoner.

You try making sounds at the nearest creature. It stops pacing and stares at you through the barrier. It makes a low, mournful sound in return. You don't share a language, but you share a situation. It returns to pacing.
Your hand gets within inches before the hair on your arm stands up. The barrier is invisible but the static charge is unmistakable. Touching it would be unwise.
The barrier emitters are embedded in the ceiling and floor. Whatever powers them is deep inside the ship's walls.

objects.name: Scratch Marks
objects.description: Deep scratches gouged into the ventilation shaft walls — previous escape attempts.

then.text: Deep gouges in the organic walls, made by claws or tools. Someone else navigated these vents before you. The scratches form patterns — not random panic, but deliberate markings. Arrows, symbols, a crude map of the shaft system. A junction ahead splits left and right. The left path is marked with a helmet symbol. The right has deep warning gouges.

You trace the scratch-map with your fingers, memorizing the layout. A junction ahead splits two ways: LEFT is marked with a helmet symbol and leads eventually to the airlock. RIGHT is gouged with warning marks — a dead end. Whoever made this got further than the Choir expected.
"Something clawed at this wall... desperately," you whisper. The scratches are too deep to have been made by human fingernails.
The scratches are gouged into the wall itself. Whatever made them is long gone.

objects.name: Security Console
objects.description: The main control station for containment deck security. Multiple screens show surveillance feeds.

then.text: You lean in to examine the security console up close...
The console is fused to the floor by thick cables of organic conduit. It's not going anywhere.
You mutter the alien symbols on the display under your breath. None of them resolve into anything meaningful, but a few recur — status codes, maybe. Or countdown timers.

objects.name: Cracked Surveillance Screen
objects.description: One of the surveillance screens is badly cracked — someone or something fought here.

then.text: The screen is cracked in a starburst pattern — something impacted it hard. The surrounding console has scorch marks. A chair is knocked over nearby. Someone fought the Choir here. The Choir won, obviously. But whoever it was put up a fight.
You trace the crack with your finger. The glass is warm — not from heat, but from whatever bioluminescent process still lights the display from within.
The screen is embedded in the console housing. Prying it out would take tools you don't have.
The fractured display flickers between two images — a schematic of the ship's lower decks and something that might be a manifest. Both are too corrupted to read clearly.

objects.name: Security Drawer
objects.description: A drawer beneath the security console, partially jammed open.

then.text: A drawer beneath the security console, jammed partially open. You can see key cards inside — but you'd need to get closer to the console to reach them properly.
You reach for the drawer, but the angle is awkward from here. You need to get up close to the console itself — lean over it and look properly.

interactions.response: A faint label above the drawer slot — three alien glyphs and what looks like a security clearance level.

objects.name: Data Crystal Archive
objects.description: Floor-to-ceiling racks of glowing data crystals — each one a species' complete biological record.

then.text: Thousands of data crystals, each humming at a slightly different frequency. The collection spans millennia — some crystals are ancient, their glow faded. Others are bright and new. Each one represents an entire species, catalogued and filed. A library of extinction.

You pull a crystal at random and slot it into the reading device. An alien species fills the holographic display — six-legged, fur-covered, intelligent eyes. Below it: a world, lush and green. And the red symbol. Consumed. You replace the crystal, feeling sick.
"A library of the dead," you whisper. Each crystal holds someone's memories, someone's life — catalogued and shelved like specimens.
The rack is a lattice of hardened organic resin, fused to the wall. The crystals sit in purpose-grown slots.

objects.name: Misplaced Data Crystal
objects.description: A crystal that's slightly different from the others — personal records rather than specimen data.

then.text: This crystal is different — smaller, a different hue. It's been misfiled among the specimen records. When you hold it up to the light, it pulses with a more complex pattern. Personal data, not biological. A Choir officer's private log, perhaps.

You pocket the crystal. It contains notation you can't read yet — alien script mixed with mathematical sequences. But there are patterns here that look like a translation key. Fragment one of something larger. If you can find more fragments, you might be able to read what the Choir writes.
"Someone recorded this. Someone who was here before me." The crystal pulses faintly, as if eager to share its secrets.
The crystal is small enough to carry. You could take it — if you can get it free from its slot.

objects.name: Crystal Reading Device
objects.description: A pedestal-mounted device for reading data crystals, projecting holographic content.

then.text: A crystalline reading device on an ornate pedestal. Slot a data crystal in and it projects the contents as a hologram above. The interface seems universal — it displays whatever species' biology is recorded on the crystal. Efficient, clinical, deeply impersonal.

You slot the personal log crystal into the reader. A flood of alien text fills the air — dense, layered, incomprehensible. But between the text: diagrams, star maps, what look like personal sketches. This Choir officer was methodical, recording everything. And buried in the notation — translation keys. Partial ones. You'd need more fragments to complete the cipher, but this is a start.
You run your fingers over the device's surface. It hums to life briefly, projecting a flicker of alien text before going dark again. It needs a crystal inserted to function.
"If I can find a crystal that fits, I might learn something useful." The device's empty slot seems to confirm your theory.
The reading device is a console grown from the archive wall. Thick neural cables feed into its base.

You pour stasis fluid into the reader's intake reservoir. The device whirs to life with renewed energy — the fluid is a power source, or at least a catalyst. The holographic projection brightens significantly. Now when you insert crystals, the reader can decode deeper layers of data. Whatever the Choir recorded, you'll see more of it.

You slot the specimen tag into the reader. A holographic display projects your biological data — heart rate, neural mapping, cellular composition. And a classification: 'Sol-3 Primate, Batch 7, Priority: LOW.' You're cataloged. A specimen in their collection, not even a high-priority one. The tag also shows a batch processing schedule. Batch 7 is next.

objects.name: Cataloguer Robot
objects.description: A spider-legged machine perched among the pods, methodically scanning and cataloguing specimens. Its amber specimen jars glow with a sickly light.

then.text: A biomechanical spider-drone clings to the far wall among the pods, methodically scanning specimens. Its amber jars hold preserved creatures — the data plates on each one catch your eye, numerical readouts alongside alien script. But it's on the other side of that gap in the walkway. You can't get close enough to read anything from here.

Now that you're close, you can see the data plates clearly. Alien script you can't read — but the numbers are universal. Each jar is labeled with a code: 7319-101, 7319-102, 7319-103. The prefix is the same across all three. Section code 7319. That could be useful.
You've already noted the section code from the specimen plates — 7-3-1-9.
The cataloguer emits a low electronic hum as it works. It doesn't respond to your voice — this machine operates on instinct, not intelligence. Just a collector, endlessly sorting the ship's trophies.

objects.name: Velith Ammonite
objects.description: Specimen 7319-101: a Velith Ammonite — a deep-ocean cephalopod with a coiled nautilus shell and dozens of sinuous tentacles, suspended in swirling amber preservative.

then.text: The Velith Ammonite floats in the amber fluid — part octopus, part nautilus, with a coiled ridged shell and dozens of sinuous arms. Its skin shifts color even in preservation, iridescent patterns rippling across the surface. The green display below scrolls alien glyphs alongside a specimen number: 7319-101.
The glass is warm to the touch and faintly vibrates. The ammonite's shell rotates a fraction of a turn in the fluid — you pull your hand back. Was that the ship's hum, or is it still alive in there?
You mutter something to the spiral shell. It doesn't respond. Of course it doesn't. But for a moment the chambers glow brighter, one after another, like a sequence trying to answer.

objects.name: Kethrani Weaver
objects.description: Specimen 7319-102: a Kethrani Weaver — a massive arachnoid predator with eight jointed legs, armored carapace, and mandibles that could crush bone, preserved in amber fluid.

then.text: The Kethrani Weaver fills the center tank — eight jointed legs spread wide, a segmented carapace with chitinous ridges, and mandibles that could crush bone. It's bigger than you are. The green display below scrolls alien glyphs alongside a specimen number: 7319-102. Whatever world this came from, you're glad you weren't there.

You press your palm flat against the glass. One of its eight legs twitches — a reflex, surely — and the mandibles click together once. A bubble rises from somewhere beneath the carapace. You pull back. Is this thing still alive in there?

"What happened to you?" you whisper. The Weaver's compound eyes stare back — hundreds of dark facets, each one reflecting a tiny version of your face. Its mandibles are frozen mid-spread, as if it was about to strike when the preservative took hold. You wonder how fast it was.

objects.name: Neural Orchid
objects.description: Specimen 7319-103: a Neural Orchid — an alien plant with layered burgundy petals and thick root tendrils, preserved in golden fluid. It blurs the line between flora and fauna.

then.text: Not an animal — a plant. Or something that blurs the line. The Neural Orchid has layered petals in deep burgundy, and thick root tendrils that curl through the amber fluid like searching fingers. The green display reads: 7319-103. A botanical specimen from some alien world, preserved perfectly. The petals seem to open slightly as you watch.

You tap the glass. The orchid's root tendrils drift toward your finger, drawn by the vibration. The petals spread wider — almost hungrily — revealing a dark core pulsing with faint bioluminescence. The Convergence collects everything, and this one looks like it might collect you back if it could.
