"You're beautiful," you whisper to the orchid. And it is — alien and deadly-looking, but beautiful. The petals flutter faintly, as if responding to your voice. You wonder if it's some kind of symbiont — something that attracts, and then feeds. The Choir might have plucked it from a garden. Or a trap.

objects.name: Specimen Displays
objects.description: Three glowing teal screens below the tanks, scrolling alien glyphs and biological data alongside specimen ID numbers.

then.text: Each tank has a teal display screen at its base, scrolling alien glyphs you can't decipher — biological classifications, feeding schedules, who knows. But alongside the glyphs, numbers. Universal, unmistakable numbers. The screens read: 7319-101, 7319-102, 7319-103. The first four digits are the same on every display.
The specimen displays still scroll their alien data alongside the numbers: 7319-101, 7319-102, 7319-103. You've already memorized the section code: 7-3-1-9.

You trace your finger along the numbers on each screen: 7319-101... 7319-102... 7319-103. The first four digits repeat on every display — that's not a specimen ID, it's a section code. 7-3-1-9. A code that repeats on every specimen. Worth remembering — it must unlock something on this ship.
You've already noted the section code: 7-3-1-9. The displays continue scrolling their alien data, but you've got what you need.

You read the numbers aloud: "Seven... three... one... nine." Your voice sounds small against the hum of the specimen tanks. The Ammonite's tentacles stir faintly in its fluid. Even it seems to be listening.

objects.name: Holographic Planet Display
objects.description: Holographic projections of cataloged worlds drifting slowly above the archive, most marked in red.

then.text: Dozens of planets drift overhead in miniature hologram — lush worlds, ice worlds, gas giants with inhabited moons. Almost all are marked with the red consumption symbol. The scale is staggering. The Convergence hasn't consumed dozens of worlds. It has consumed hundreds. Thousands. Across galaxies, across epochs. This archive stretches back billions of years.
Your hand passes through the holographic projection. The display flickers and reconfigures around your fingers, unbothered.
"Some kind of catalog system," you say, watching alien glyphs scroll past. The display shifts in response to your voice, but you can't read any of it.
The display is a projection — there's nothing physical to move. The emitter is embedded somewhere in the ceiling.

You hold the neural tendril up to the holographic display. The tendril twitches — still faintly alive — and the display responds, reconfiguring around this new biological input. The star map zooms in, planet after planet flickering past, until it locks on a single system. A single yellow star. Eight planets. Third from the sun. The Convergence's next destination. Your home system. They're heading for Earth. The tendril goes dark in your hand, spent. But you've learned what you needed to know.

objects.name: Viewport
objects.description: A large viewport showing the planet below — beautiful from orbit, unaware it's dying.

then.text: The planet fills the viewport. Blue oceans, green continents, wisps of white cloud. From up here it looks healthy, alive, beautiful. But you can see them now — thin beams of light descending from orbit to the surface. Energy siphons. The Convergence is already feeding. The planet doesn't know it's dying.
The viewport glass is ice-cold to the touch. Your fingerprints fog and fade in the chill radiating from the void beyond.
"That's the way out," you murmur, staring into the star-flecked darkness. If only it were that simple.
The viewport is a thick slab of transparent alloy set flush into the hull. It isn't going anywhere.

objects.name: Empty Docking Clamps
objects.description: Heavy mechanical clamps Something was docked here — the outline in the wear pattern looks familiar. The clamps are open and empty.

then.text: The docking clamps are open, still showing the outline of your ship's hull in wear patterns. The docking clamps are open, still showing the outline of a ship's hull in wear patterns. Something about the shape tugs at your memory — your ship? A name surfaces: Outrider. Your ship. Your way out. Jettisoned. Probably automated: the Choir don't want escape vehicles lying around for specimens to find. Your ship is gone. You're not leaving this way.
The docking clamps are massive hydraulic mechanisms. Your hands can barely wrap around one of the smaller guide rails.
"Whatever was docked here left in a hurry," you observe. The clamps are still in their release position.
Each clamp is anchored to the deck with bolts thicker than your wrist. They're not moving.

objects.name: Emergency Suit Locker
objects.description: A locker containing alien emergency space suits, designed for the crew's physiology.

then.text: Emergency suit locker, cracked open from whatever impact rocked the ship. The suits inside are designed for the crew's physiology. You already have the helmet from the security hub — the only piece that fits you.
Emergency suit locker — standard safety equipment near an airlock. The suits inside are sized for the ship's crew: far too large for you. But the helmets...

You pull the locker open. Three Choir emergency suits hang inside — massive, organic-looking, completely unwearable for someone your size. But the helmets are modular, designed to seal independently. One might fit you, barely, worn like an oversized bucket on your head.
You pull the smallest helmet free. It's still too big, but the internal padding can be adjusted. It'll protect against vacuum, toxins, and energy bursts — at least briefly. Better than nothing.
"Emergency EVA equipment," you read from the faded label. The alien script beneath it probably says the same thing.
The suit locker is welded to the bulkhead. Standard safety protocol — even on alien ships, apparently.

objects.name: Manual Override Panel
objects.description: A heavily locked manual override panel for the airlock blast doors.

then.text: A manual override panel for the airlock doors, covered by heavy bio-organic locks. Even if you opened it, the blast doors lead to vacuum — and your ship isn't on the other side anymore. But the override circuitry might be useful for other purposes.
The locks are bio-organic and heavy — designed to prevent accidental decompression. You can't force them open with your bare hands.

The containment key card interfaces with the lock. The panel opens, revealing override controls. You won't be using the airlock itself — but you've learned how the ship's override systems work. This knowledge will help with other locked systems.
"Emergency override... if I can figure out the sequence." The panel's symbols glow faintly, waiting for input.
The override panel is integrated into the airlock frame itself. It can't be removed.

objects.name: Sealed Blast Doors
objects.description: Heavy organic-metallic blast doors sealing the airlock from the corridor.

then.text: Massive blast doors designed to contain decompression. These lead to the outer airlock — and beyond that, vacuum. They're sealed for a reason. Even if you could open them, there's nothing on the other side but death.
You press your palms against the blast doors. They're sealed tight — several inches of reinforced alloy standing between you and the airlock chamber.
"These doors are the last barrier," you say quietly. Beyond them lies the airlock, and beyond that — freedom or the void.
The blast doors weigh several tons. No amount of pushing will budge them without the override.

objects.name: Holographic Star Map
objects.description: A massive hologram showing the Convergence's path across galaxies — hundreds of consumed systems marked in red.

then.text: Hundreds of star systems traced in light, spanning multiple galaxies. The consumed ones glow red — there are so many they form a trail, a path of destruction stretching back across cosmic time. The current system pulses amber: in progress. Not yet consumed. Not yet dead.

You manipulate the star map controls, zooming into the local cluster. Your home system is visible — unmarked, untouched, ignorant. The path of consumption hasn't reached it yet. But the trajectory is clear. It will. You memorize key coordinates and navigation data.

interactions.response: You can't move the Star Map.
Talking to the Star Map yields no response.

objects.name: Command Console
objects.description: The primary command station, grown into the floor like a mushroom. Navigation controls and the ship's flight systems.

then.text: The command console is a bio-organic workstation grown from the floor, its surface covered in responsive membranes and neural interfaces. A navigation chip slot is visible — the ship's course is set by physical media, not software. Remove the chip, change the course.

You reach into the navigation slot and extract a small crystalline chip — the ship's current course data, including coordinates for the nearest relay stations and jump points. With this chip and a working shuttle, you could navigate out of this system.

interactions.response: The Console won't budge.
You fiddle with the Console. It accomplishes nothing.
The Console has nothing to say.

objects.name: Command Throne
objects.description: A seat designed for the ship's commander, with neural interface tendrils hanging from a headrest.

then.text: The command throne is massive — built for a Choir commander twice your height. Neural interface tendrils hang from the headrest like limp tentacles, waiting to connect to a Choir's nervous system. Through that connection, the commander would feel the entire ship as an extension of their body.

You press the severed tendril against the throne's interface port. For a flash, you feel the ship — a vast, cold awareness. Corridors like veins. The reactor like a heart. The Curator's precise footsteps somewhere below. Then the connection breaks. The tendril doesn't have enough bio-electricity to maintain it. But you felt it — the ship is alive, and it knows you're aboard.

interactions.response: You can't move the Throne.
You prod the Throne. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Throne. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Organic Reactor
objects.description: A massive pulsing organic reactor — like a beating heart wrapped in mechanical cables and transparent coolant tubes.

then.text: The reactor is a living thing — a heart the size of a house, wrapped in mechanical supports and coolant systems. With each pulse, the entire room shudders. Transparent tubes carry glowing coolant through a circulatory system. The vibration masks most sounds in here — good for hiding, terrible for hearing someone approach.

interactions.response: Moving the Reactor would accomplish nothing.
You poke at the Reactor. No reaction.
You address the Reactor. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Reactor Access Panel
objects.description: A maintenance panel on the reactor housing, where power cells are installed and removed.

then.text: A maintenance access panel on the reactor casing. Behind it, power cells are slotted into the reactor's distribution grid — portable energy sources that can be removed and used elsewhere. The panel is held shut by organic fasteners.

You pry the fasteners loose and swing the panel open. Inside: a grid of power cells, each glowing with stored reactor energy. Most are locked into the grid, but one on the edge can be disconnected without triggering a system alert.

You carefully disconnect the edge power cell. It comes free with a click and a brief flicker in the lighting — the reactor compensates almost instantly. The cell is warm, heavy, and full of energy. This could power a shuttle... or anything else that needs a boost.

interactions.response: The Panel is firmly in place.
You mutter something at the Panel. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Coolant Distribution System
objects.description: Transparent tubes carrying glowing coolant through the engineering bay.

then.text: Glowing blue coolant flows through transparent tubes, keeping the reactor from overheating. The tubes branch and merge in patterns that look almost organic — because they are. The coolant itself is bio-active, a living fluid that absorbs and dissipates heat.

You find a maintenance flask near a junction point and fill it from a coolant bleed valve. The blue liquid is ice-cold despite the surrounding heat. Useful for cooling overheated systems — or as an emergency weapon. The stuff freezes on contact with warm surfaces.

interactions.response: Moving the Coolant would accomplish nothing.
You poke at the Coolant. No reaction.
You address the Coolant. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Power Distribution Panel
objects.description: A toggle panel controlling power distribution across the ship's operational systems.

then.text: A panel of bio-organic toggles controlling power distribution across the ship. Each toggle routes reactor energy to different systems: life support, weapons, navigation, shuttle bay, communications. Currently all systems are powered. Redirecting power could create opportunities — and risks.

You study the toggle layout. Routing extra power to the shuttle bay would speed launch prep, but the power has to come from somewhere. You could reduce weapons systems — the Choir would notice eventually, but it would buy time. You carefully reroute power to the shuttle bay systems.

interactions.response: The Toggles is firmly in place.
You mutter something at the Toggles. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Communications Dish
objects.description: A dish-like apparatus suspended in the center of the room, surrounded by crystalline amplifiers.

then.text: The dish apparatus channels the Choir's subsonic communications across vast distances. Crystalline amplifiers boost the signal, turning thought-vibrations into interstellar transmissions. Through this array, the Choir reports to the Convergence. Every species catalogued, every planet consumed — logged and transmitted.

interactions.response: Moving the Dish would accomplish nothing.
You poke at the Dish. No reaction.
You address the Dish. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Recording Station
objects.description: Where the Choir logs its reports to the Convergence. A strange microphone-like device and data storage.

then.text: A recording station where the Choir dictates mission reports. The 'microphone' is a resonance sensor that captures subsonic vibrations. Stored reports are kept on crystalline media — and one storage unit contains something different. A ship's black box recorder, standard deep-space salvage equipment. Your black box. From the Outrider.

You pull the Outrider's black box from the storage unit. It's human tech — your tech — scratched and battered but intact. It contains your ship's logs: your identity, your mission, your species' existence. Proof that you came here on purpose, not as livestock. Proof of sentience.

interactions.response: The Recorder is firmly in place.
You run your hands over the Recorder. Nothing of interest.
You speak to the Recorder. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Schematic Display
objects.description: Technical displays showing the communications array's internal architecture and transmission protocols.

then.text: Technical schematics for the communications array — transmission frequencies, amplifier configurations, targeting protocols. This is how the Choir talks to the stars. With these schematics, someone could build — or hijack — a transmission system.

You extract the schematic data onto a portable crystal. The comm array's blueprints — frequencies, power requirements, targeting algorithms. With this and enough power, you could broadcast on the Convergence's own network. Send a message to anyone listening.

interactions.response: You strain against the Schematics. It doesn't move.
You touch the Schematics. Nothing happens.
Talking to the Schematics yields no response.

objects.name: Frequency Dial
objects.description: A dial for tuning the comm array's transmission frequency. Currently locked to the Convergence's channel.

then.text: A frequency dial locked to the Convergence's communication channel. Tuning it to a different frequency could intercept other transmissions — or let you eavesdrop on the Convergence's own communications. The correct intercept frequency is probably in the bridge's navigation data.
The dial has hundreds of positions. Without knowing the correct frequency, you'd be tuning blind. The bridge's star charts might contain frequency data for Convergence communications channels.

Using the frequency data from the bridge's star charts, you tune the dial to the Convergence's primary command channel. Static resolves into subsonic patterns — you can't understand them, but the array's translation buffer renders a partial decode. Communications about the harvest's progress. Timetables. And coordinates for other harvesting operations across the galaxy.

interactions.response: The Dial won't budge.
You speak to the Dial. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Weapons Rack
objects.description: Racks of Choir weapons — resonance staffs, energy projectors, containment nets. Most are biometrically locked.

then.text: Racks of Choir weapons — elegant, lethal, and completely useless to you. Each one is biometrically locked to its assigned handler's physiology. The resonance staffs hum when you approach. The energy projectors are too heavy to lift. But one device near the bottom looks different — smaller, more tool than weapon.

You pull the small device from the rack — a resonance disruptor. Not a weapon exactly, but a tool that disrupts bio-organic mechanisms. It vibrates in your hand, countering the frequencies that Choir tech uses. Locks, barriers, organic circuits — this thing scrambles them all.

interactions.response: You strain against the Weapons. It doesn't move.
You touch the Weapons. Nothing happens.
Talking to the Weapons yields no response.

objects.name: Weapon Maintenance Bench
objects.description: A workbench for maintaining and repairing Choir weapons.

then.text: Tools for maintaining bio-organic weaponry — tuning forks, growth accelerants, resonance calibrators. A damaged weapon sits half-disassembled, its innards exposed. The Choir maintains its arsenal with surgical precision.

interactions.response: The Workbench won't budge.
You fiddle with the Workbench. It accomplishes nothing.
The Workbench has nothing to say.

objects.name: Empty Rack Slot
objects.description: A gap in the weapon rack where something was recently removed.

then.text: A gap in the rack where a weapon was removed recently — the mounting hooks are still warm. Whatever was here, the Curator took it. Recently. That means the Curator is armed with something beyond its natural manipulators. Be careful.

interactions.response: You can't move the Gap.
You prod the Gap. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Gap. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Resonance Chamber
objects.description: A circular depression in the floor that glows with subsonic energy — the Choir's communal communication space.

then.text: The resonance chamber is how the Choir speaks — not with words but with vibrations. Standing at the edge, you feel patterns in the subsonic hum: data, emotions, shared memory. Among the patterns, something stands out — a translation matrix. The Choir learned this world's languages when they arrived. A fragment of that learning is encoded in the chamber's resonance.

You step into the chamber and let the vibrations wash over you. Among the subsonic noise, you isolate a pattern — a translation fragment, the Choir's Rosetta Stone for this region of space. Combined with other fragments, it could decode alien text across multiple species. Fragment two of the translation cipher.

interactions.response: Moving the Chamber would accomplish nothing.
The Chamber has nothing to say.

objects.name: Dormant Choir Members
objects.description: Choir members standing motionless in wall alcoves, connected to the ship by neural tendrils from their backs.

then.text: Tall, eyeless figures standing upright in alcoves, neural tendrils connecting their spines to the ship's walls. They're dormant — not sleeping exactly, but in a low-power state, their consciousness merged with the ship's systems. They dream in data. One twitches occasionally, its manipulator limbs flexing in some automated reflex.

You reach toward the nearest dormant Choir member and immediately think better of it. Its skin is warm, faintly vibrating. The neural tendrils pulse with data. Touching it might alert the others — or the ship itself.

interactions.response: You can't move the Dormant.
Talking to the Dormant yields no response.

objects.name: Wall Patterns
objects.description: Intricate geometric patterns covering the walls — art, language, or something else entirely.

then.text: Geometric patterns cover every surface — nested triangles, spiraling fractals, interlocking hexagons. Art? Language? Navigation? Without understanding Choir communication, you can only guess. The patterns shift subtly if you stare too long, responding to the resonance chamber's vibrations.

With the complete translation cipher, the patterns resolve into meaning. It's all three — art, language, and navigation. The walls tell the Choir's history: their creation by the Convergence, their purpose, their travels. There's a note of pride in the patterns. And buried deep, something that might be doubt.

interactions.response: The Patterns won't budge.
You fiddle with the Patterns. It accomplishes nothing.
The Patterns has nothing to say.

objects.name: Damaged Shuttle
objects.description: A beetle-shaped shuttle with panels removed and visible damage — missing its power cell.

then.text: The middle shuttle is the one in worst shape — panels removed, internal systems exposed. The power cell bay is empty, fuel lines disconnected, navigation offline. But the hull is intact and the launch mechanism works. With the right components, this thing could fly.
The shuttle hums with restored power. Fuel lines connected, navigation initialized. It's ready to fly — straight down to the planet below. This is your ticket off this ship. One-way.

You slot the reactor power cell into the shuttle's empty bay. Systems flicker to life — emergency lighting, basic avionics, status displays. The shuttle has power. But it still needs fuel and navigation to fly.
You reconnect the fuel line, routing propellant from the bay's fuel system to the shuttle's engines. The fuel gauge climbs. Enough for a one-way trip to the planet's surface — barely.

You insert the navigation chip. The shuttle's systems fully initialize — a holographic display shows the planet below, landing zones calculated. The shuttle is repaired. Ready to launch. The bay doors will open on command. This is it.

interactions.response: You can't move the Shuttle.
You prod the Shuttle. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Shuttle. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Shuttle Bay Supply Rack
objects.description: A rack of spare parts and supplies for shuttle maintenance.

then.text: Spare parts for shuttle maintenance: replacement panels, sealant tubes, calibration tools. And fuel lines — coiled and labeled. One matches the gauge of the damaged shuttle's disconnected fuel system.
You pull a replacement fuel line from the rack. It's the right gauge for the damaged shuttle — flexible organic tubing that connects the bay's fuel supply to the shuttle's engines.

interactions.response: Moving the Supplies would accomplish nothing.
You poke at the Supplies. No reaction.
You address the Supplies. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Launch Controls
objects.description: Bay door and launch mechanism controls in a booth overlooking the shuttle bay.

then.text: Launch controls in the overhead booth — bay door operation, launch cradle release, atmospheric containment. From here you could open the bay to space and launch a shuttle. The controls are surprisingly straightforward — the Choir designed for efficiency, not security.

You activate the launch sequence. Alarms blare — bay doors cycling open. The containment field shimmers as atmosphere holds inside the bay while space yawns beyond. The shuttle's cradle unlocks. This is the point of no return. Board the shuttle, and you're heading for the planet.

interactions.response: The Launch is firmly in place.
You mutter something at the Launch. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Harvest Station
objects.description: A station for harvesting biological material from the garden's plants.

then.text: Curved cutting tools and collection vessels for harvesting plant materials. The station processes extracts used throughout the ship — medicines, sealants, nutrients. The bio-garden is the ship's pharmacy, its factory, its pantry.

You operate the harvest station, collecting a vial of concentrated plant extract. The liquid is deep green and smells of life — the purest biological substance on this ship. It has restorative properties and is a key ingredient in Choir bio-chemistry.

interactions.response: Moving the Harvest would accomplish nothing.
You poke at the Harvest. No reaction.
You address the Harvest. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Fibrous Plants
objects.description: Tall, reed-like plants producing strong organic fibers used in ship construction.

then.text: Tall reed-like plants swaying in the nutrient bath. Their stems produce incredibly strong fibers — the same material used in the ship's internal structures. Harvest the fibers and they could reinforce almost anything.
You strip fibers from several reed stems. They're surprisingly strong — like carbon fiber but organic. Wound tightly, they could reinforce a blade, bind components together, or serve as cordage.

interactions.response: The Fibers is firmly in place.
You run your hands over the Fibers. Nothing of interest.
You speak to the Fibers. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Carnivorous Plant
objects.description: A large plant with a maw-like flower that tracks your movement.

then.text: The maw-like flower turns to follow you as you move. It's the size of your torso, lined with digestive cilia. The Choir probably grows these as waste disposal or pest control. You're exactly the right size to be 'pest.'
You reach toward the plant experimentally. The maw SNAPS shut, missing your hand by inches. It reopens slowly, cilia waving hungrily. That's a hard no.

interactions.response: You strain against the Hungry Plant. It doesn't move.
You address the Hungry Plant. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Brain Interface Terminal
objects.description: One of several terminals around the perimeter for interfacing with the ship's organic brain.

then.text: A terminal for querying the ship's organic brain. Neural cables connect it to the central tank. The interface uses resonance patterns — not keyboards, but vibration-sensitive membranes. Through this terminal, you could access the ship's entire database.

You press your palms against the vibration membranes. Data floods through — too fast, too alien. But you catch fragments: navigation logs, specimen catalogs, maintenance schedules. And resonance frequencies — the crystal harmonics the Choir uses for everything. One crystal in the terminal's output tray contains raw resonance data. You take it.

interactions.response: The Terminal is firmly in place.
You mutter something at the Terminal. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Organic Brain
objects.description: The ship's central computer — a massive brain suspended in translucent fluid, pulsing with thought.

then.text: It fills the tank — folds and ridges of neural tissue, glowing with bio-electric patterns. Neural cables radiate from it in every direction, connecting to every system on the ship. It processes, thinks, dreams. It knows the location of every door, every camera, every specimen. Including you. You can feel it watching, in its alien way.

You try speaking to the brain. Nothing. It doesn't communicate that way. But the vibration membranes on the terminal shimmer in response to your voice — it heard you. It just doesn't care. You're a specimen, not a person. Not to it.

interactions.response: Moving the Brain would accomplish nothing.
You poke at the Brain. No reaction.

objects.name: Maintenance Drone
objects.description: A small spider-like drone skittering across surfaces, performing automated repairs.

then.text: A spider-like maintenance drone the size of a cat. Eight articulated legs, a cluster of sensor eyes, tool-appendages for welding and cutting. It ignores you completely — you're not a maintenance issue. Not yet.

You grab the drone mid-scuttle. It squeals — a high-pitched mechanical whine — and struggles. You manage to snap off its antenna before it wriggles free and skitters away, broadcasting alarm signals. That'll attract attention.

interactions.response: You can't move the Drone.
Talking to the Drone yields no response.

objects.name: Catwalks
objects.description: Metal catwalks spanning over grinders and acid baths in the waste processing facility.

then.text: Narrow catwalks cross over the machinery below — grinders, acid baths, reprocessing vats. The catwalks connect the engineering section to the hive quarters, a shortcut between decks. It's dangerous, loud, and no one comes here voluntarily. Perfect.

interactions.response: The Catwalks won't budge.
You fiddle with the Catwalks. It accomplishes nothing.
The Catwalks has nothing to say.

objects.name: Grinders
objects.description: Massive industrial grinders below the catwalks, breaking down waste material.

then.text: The grinders churn constantly, reducing waste material to pulp. The noise is tremendous — the loudest area on the ship. Anything dropped in wouldn't last a second. The good news: the noise here masks everything else. The Curator can't hear you over this din.

interactions.response: You can't move the Grinders.
You prod the Grinders. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Grinders. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Observation Instruments
objects.description: Alien instruments for observing and measuring the planet and the harvesting operation.

then.text: Observation instruments trained on the planet below — energy output readings, atmospheric composition, biomass calculations. The Convergence tracks exactly how much life force it's draining. Current extraction: 12.7%. The planet can survive up to about 40% before cascading ecosystem collapse. They're methodical about it. Taking just enough, at just the right rate, to maximize yield.

interactions.response: Moving the Instruments would accomplish nothing.
You poke at the Instruments. No reaction.
You address the Instruments. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Panoramic Viewport
objects.description: A massive viewport showing the planet below and the Convergence's energy siphon beams descending from orbit.

then.text: The planet fills the viewport — a world of blue oceans and green continents, achingly beautiful. But the energy siphons are visible now: dozens of thin white beams descending from orbital platforms to the surface. Where they touch, the atmosphere yellows. Clouds dissolve. The oceans dim. A world being slowly murdered from orbit. Beautiful and horrifying simultaneously.

interactions.response: The Viewport is firmly in place.
You run your hands over the Viewport. Nothing of interest.
You speak to the Viewport. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Shuttle Dashboard
objects.description: The crashed shuttle's instrument panel. Most systems are dead, but some emergency functions still flicker.

then.text: Most instruments are dead — cracked screens, severed cables. But the emergency beacon system still has power, its indicator blinking amber. The navigation display is damaged but partially readable, showing your crash coordinates. If you could signal the shuttle, it might be able to lift off on autopilot... if you're not inside it.

You pry the emergency beacon module from the dashboard. It's self-contained — its own power source, its own transmitter. Press the button and it broadcasts a recall signal to the shuttle's autopilot. One-use only. The shuttle would attempt to launch and fly to the beacon's coordinates. Escape in a box.

interactions.response: You strain against the Dashboard. It doesn't move.
You touch the Dashboard. Nothing happens.
Talking to the Dashboard yields no response.

objects.name: Emergency Kit
objects.description: A scattered emergency kit — supplies thrown around the cockpit during the crash.

then.text: Emergency supplies scattered during impact: alien first aid components, a Choir-standard signal flare, nutrition packs (empty). The signal flare is still intact — a chemical light source that burns bright enough to be seen from orbit.
You pocket the signal flare. Choir-standard emergency equipment — chemical ignition, burns for about ten minutes at blinding intensity. Useful as a light source, a distraction, or a signal. One shot.

interactions.response: The Kit won't budge.
You fiddle with the Kit. It accomplishes nothing.
The Kit has nothing to say.

objects.name: Personal Items
objects.description: Items from the Outrider that somehow ended up in the shuttle — a photo, a mug, familiar objects from another life.

then.text: A photograph — you and someone, somewhere warm, smiling. A coffee mug with a chip on the rim. Small things from the Outrider that the Choir must have stored with your other belongings. Evidence of a life before this. You stare at the photo for a long time.

interactions.response: You can't move the Keepsakes.
You prod the Keepsakes. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Keepsakes. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Crashed Shuttle Hull
objects.description: The beetle-shaped shuttle half-buried in grey soil, one wing sheared off, smoke still rising.

then.text: The shuttle came down hard — one wing is gone, the hull crumpled on impact. Grey soil piled against the nose where it plowed a furrow across the wasteland. It won't fly again in this state, but the cockpit is relatively intact. Might still have useful supplies inside.

interactions.response: Moving the Wreckage would accomplish nothing.
You poke at the Wreckage. No reaction.
You address the Wreckage. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Crystal Deposit
objects.description: Crystalline mineral growths at the base of the siphon tower, formed by the Convergence's energy mineralization.

then.text: The ground around the tower base is covered in crystalline mineral deposits — the soil itself transformed by centuries of energy saturation. The minerals shimmer with absorbed planetary energy. They're warm to the touch, faintly radioactive, and unique to harvesting sites.

You chip off a sample of the crystallized mineral. It's warm in your hand, pulsing faintly with stored energy. This mineral has absorbed the Convergence's harvesting energy for years — it might be useful for dampening or redirecting that same energy.

interactions.response: The Minerals is firmly in place.
You run your hands over the Minerals. Nothing of interest.
You speak to the Minerals. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Siphon Crystal Spire
objects.description: The base of the massive siphon tower. Energy crackles across its surface. A fragment could be broken off — carefully or otherwise.

then.text: The siphon tower rises hundreds of meters above you — a crystalline spire of compressed energy. Up close, you can see stress fractures where the crystal has grown unevenly. A fragment from this tower would contain raw Convergence energy — incredibly powerful, incredibly dangerous. You could break a piece off with force... or cut one free precisely.

You strike the crystal at a stress fracture with all your strength. A piece breaks free with a DEAFENING crack that echoes across the wasteland. Energy discharges wildly for a moment. Your hands tingle painfully. But you have it — a shard of raw Convergence crystal, pulsing with stolen planetary energy.

You score the crystal along a natural stress line with the reinforced blade, working the cut deeper with patient precision. After several minutes, a clean fragment separates with a soft chime — much quieter than brute force. The crystal pulses in your hand, warm with stolen energy.

interactions.response: You strain against the Spire. It doesn't move.
You address the Spire. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Scattered Belongings
objects.description: Personal possessions left behind by refugees — clothing, tools, keepsakes, records.

then.text: Scattered across the campsite: clothing sized for four-armed beings, alien tools and utensils, children's toys, data tablets. Among the debris, a journal-like device — a personal record kept by one of the refugees. Its power cell still holds a charge.

You pick up the journal device. It contains a refugee's account of the final days — the Convergence arriving, the evacuation failing, the desperate flight from the city. And buried in the entries, translation notes. This refugee was a linguist, trying to decode Choir communications. Translation cipher fragment three.

interactions.response: The Belongings is firmly in place.
You run your hands over the Belongings. Nothing of interest.
You speak to the Belongings. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Supply Crate
objects.description: A sealed supply crate among the refugee camp supplies, still intact.

then.text: A military-standard supply crate, still sealed. The refugee camp was partially supplied by the military before it fell. This crate is marked with symbols that look like climbing equipment and food rations.

You pry the crate open. Inside: climbing pitons designed for four-armed use but adaptable, survival ration packs, and basic medical supplies. The rations are still good — preserved with alien technology that doesn't expire.
You take the climbing pitons — alien metal, light but incredibly strong. They're designed for four hands but work fine with two. Essential for vertical terrain.
You grab the survival rations — compact packs of alien food, nutrient-dense and sealed. They taste like nothing you've ever eaten, but they'll keep you going.

interactions.response: You strain against the Crate. It doesn't move.
You address the Crate. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Fallen Refugees
objects.description: Skeletons of the planet's former inhabitants — tall, thin, four-armed — lying where they fell during the evacuation.

then.text: Tall, thin skeletons with four arms each. Some clutch bundles to their chests — belongings they refused to leave behind. Others are posed in running stances, caught mid-stride. A family group — two adults, three small ones — huddled together. They never made it out of the camp. The Convergence didn't kill them quickly. It drained their world until nothing could survive.

interactions.response: The Remains is firmly in place.
You run your hands over the Remains. Nothing of interest.
You speak to the Remains. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Bioluminescent Fungus
objects.description: A massive mushroom-like organism with a purple-blue bioluminescent cap, producing potent biological extracts.

then.text: A massive fungus with a cap the size of a table, pulsing with purple-blue bioluminescence. The underside drips with a concentrated extract — the fungus's defense mechanism, rich in bio-active compounds. These organisms survived the Convergence's harvest by growing in the rock formation's shadow, where the siphon beams couldn't reach.

You collect the dripping extract in a container. Deep purple, warm, and intensely bio-active — it makes your skin tingle on contact. Potent healing properties and useful as a biochemical reagent. The fungi don't seem to mind the harvest; they regenerate quickly.

interactions.response: You strain against the Mushroom. It doesn't move.
You touch the Mushroom. Nothing happens.
Talking to the Mushroom yields no response.

objects.name: Fungal Shelter
objects.description: A large fungus hollowed out and used as a crude shelter by survivors. A makeshift door, bedding inside.

then.text: Someone hollowed out this giant fungus and made it home. A crude door, bedding of dried spore material, scratched marks on the inner wall counting days. Whoever lived here survived for a while — the count goes past two hundred. Then stops. A relatively safe haven, but temporary. Everything on this planet is temporary now.

interactions.response: The Shelter won't budge.
You fiddle with the Shelter. It accomplishes nothing.
The Shelter has nothing to say.

objects.name: Flickering Echoes
objects.description: Ghostly translucent figures and buildings flickering in and out of existence, replaying moments from the past.

then.text: The Echoes flicker like corrupted holograms — buildings shimmer into existence, populated with translucent four-armed figures going about their daily lives. A market. A school. Children playing. Then it stutters, glitches, and you see the same scene overlaid with the moment of destruction: the sky turning yellow, the ground cracking, people running. Past and apocalypse, layered on top of each other.

The echo stabilizer's field steadies the flickering manifestations. They solidify slightly — still translucent, but now stable enough to observe clearly. One figure turns toward you. It sees you. A tall scientist, four arms clutching data tablets, mouth moving. It's trying to tell you something. Without a way to communicate, you can only read its gestures: it points toward the city gates, urgently, repeatedly.

interactions.response: You can't move the Echoes.
You prod the Echoes. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Echoes. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Bunker Door
objects.description: A heavy blast door with alien military insignia, partially open. A combination lock secures the inner chamber.

then.text: The outer blast door is forced open — whoever used this bunker didn't bother closing it when they left. But the inner armory door has a combination lock: alien military security, still powered by the bunker's generator. The code isn't obvious.

The combination lock has twelve positions in a hexagonal pattern. Without the code, you'd need to try thousands of combinations. The refugee journal mentioned military dates and protocols — and the bunker defense schematics might contain access procedures.

You enter the code derived from the refugee journal dates and bunker schematics. The lock clicks through its sequence — each position lighting green — and the inner door swings open. Inside: the bunker's armory, still stocked with the planet's last weapons.

You cross-reference the refugee journal's military dates with the notation system on the bunker door. The journal mentions 'the day the sky changed' — a specific date in the alien calendar. Combined with the defense schematics' standard military access protocols, you work out the combination.

interactions.response: Moving the Blast Door would accomplish nothing.
The Blast Door has nothing to say.

objects.name: Weapons Cache
objects.description: Racks of alien military weapons and equipment — the planet's defenders stored their last arsenal here.

then.text: Military equipment from the planet's final defense: sidearms, body armor sized for four-armed soldiers, sensor equipment, and — standing out from the conventional weapons — an echo stabilizer. The previous civilization understood the Echoes and built technology to interact with them.

You take the echo stabilizer — a device that generates a field stabilizing the Convergence's residual energy patterns. With this, you can safely interact with Echoes without them glitching into hostility. It also registers you as a 'memory pattern' rather than a living intruder — useful for getting past the city's automated defenses.

You take an alien sidearm — a compact energy weapon sized for four hands but manageable with two. The charge indicator shows limited power — maybe six shots. Use them wisely. The weapon is loud and powerful, drawing attention but eliminating threats.

interactions.response: You can't move the Weapons.
You prod the Weapons. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Weapons. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Command Table
objects.description: A tactical planning table with holographic projectors, showing the planet's last defense plans.

then.text: The holographic projectors still work — a ghostly map of the planet appears above the table. Defense positions marked, siphon tower locations plotted, and a final desperate plan outlined: an assault on the Convergence nexus using a weapon designed to turn the nexus's own energy against itself. They got as far as building prototypes.

You extract the defense schematics from the table's data store. Detailed plans for the nexus assault, weapon prototypes, troop movements. And partial blueprints for the countermeasure weapon — not complete, but a critical piece of the puzzle. Combined with the research lab's full schematics, you'd have everything needed to build it.

interactions.response: Moving the Table would accomplish nothing.
You poke at the Table. No reaction.
You address the Table. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Equipment Locker
objects.description: A military equipment locker with sensor and safety gear.

then.text: Standard military issue equipment: sensor gear, communication devices (dead), and radiation detection badges. The badges were designed to monitor exposure to Convergence energy — useful for navigating areas of high energy concentration.

You clip a radiation badge to your chest. It immediately starts registering — low background levels from the Convergence's energy field. The badge changes color with exposure: green is safe, yellow is caution, red is dangerous. Currently a steady yellow-green. It'll warn you before you walk into lethal energy zones.

interactions.response: The Locker is firmly in place.
You run your hands over the Locker. Nothing of interest.
You speak to the Locker. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Gate Archway
objects.description: The main gate archway — massive, partially collapsed, with alien reliefs and dark crystalline inlays.

then.text: The gate arch towers overhead, carved with reliefs of four-armed figures in poses of welcome and warning. Crystalline inlays that once glowed are dark and dead. The gate itself is energy-sealed — the city's automated defense system detects non-native biology and refuses entry. You need to register as something the city recognizes.

You push against the energy barrier. It crackles and pushes back — recognizing you as non-native biology. The defense system is still active after all this time, protecting a dead city from intruders. You need to fool it into thinking you belong.

You activate the echo stabilizer at the gate. Its field wraps around you, registering your biological signature as a 'memory pattern' — the same energy signature as the Echoes that drift through these ruins. The gate's defense system scans you... pauses... and accepts. The energy barrier dissolves. The dead city opens before you.

interactions.response: You strain against the Gate. It doesn't move.
You address the Gate. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Panoramic Vista
objects.description: The full scope of the planet's situation visible from the overlook — wasteland, city, and nexus.

then.text: From this height, the full scope of devastation is visible. Behind: grey wasteland stretching to the crash site. Below and ahead: the alien city, elegant spires rising from empty streets. And dominating the far horizon: the Convergence nexus. A crystal mountain, pulsing with stolen energy, with dozens of siphon beams converging on it from across the planet. The machine that kills worlds. That's where you need to go.

interactions.response: The Vista is firmly in place.
You run your hands over the Vista. Nothing of interest.
You speak to the Vista. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Petrified Vegetation
objects.description: Dead alien trees, frozen mid-growth by the energy drain, their root systems exposed like skeletal fingers.

then.text: Once-living trees, drained of all biological energy and turned to stone. The Convergence didn't just kill the vegetation — it petrified it, extracting every molecule of useful energy and leaving behind mineral husks. The root systems are exposed where the soil eroded away, reaching into empty air like grasping hands.

interactions.response: You strain against the Dead Trees. It doesn't move.
You touch the Dead Trees. Nothing happens.
Talking to the Dead Trees yields no response.

objects.name: Crystalline Growths
objects.description: Strange crystal formations where the Convergence's energy has transformed the soil into mineral structures.

then.text: Where the Convergence's energy saturated the soil most intensely, the ground has crystallized into strange mineral formations. They catch the sickly yellow-green light and refract it into unexpected rainbows. Beautiful and toxic — the radiation badge ticks faster near them.

interactions.response: The Crystals won't budge.
You fiddle with the Crystals. It accomplishes nothing.
The Crystals has nothing to say.

objects.name: Dry Fountain
objects.description: An ornamental fountain, bone-dry. The basin is cracked.

then.text: A grand fountain, now dry. The basin is cracked and filled with dust. Water channels lead to it from all directions — once this was the heart of the plaza. Coins or their alien equivalent litter the bottom.
You reach into the dry basin and sift through the dust. Your fingers find nothing of use — just faded tokens and crumbled offerings.

interactions.response: You can't move the Fountain.
Talking to the Fountain yields no response.

objects.name: Four-Armed Statue
objects.description: A towering statue of one of the planet's former inhabitants.

then.text: A tall, four-armed figure carved from pale stone. Its expression is serene, its upper arms raised in a gesture of welcome. Around its neck hangs a carved pendant — the same symbol you've seen on the library and temple. At the base, an inscription in alien script.
The inscription reads: 'We who remain welcome those who come after. Take the keystone. Remember us.' The statue's lower right hand holds a removable stone token.
You pry the stone token from the statue's hand. It's warm to the touch — a city keystone, granting access to restricted areas.

You run your hands over the stone base. The carving is exquisite — four arms in perfect proportion. The lower right hand seems to grip something, but you can't tell what without understanding the inscription.

interactions.response: The Statue won't budge.
You speak to the Statue. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Abandoned Table
objects.description: A dining table with a meal still set. The food has long since petrified.

then.text: A meal for three, frozen in time. Alien cutlery laid out — wide-handled, designed for four-armed diners. The food is petrified, grey. A drinking vessel is tipped over, its contents long evaporated. They were mid-meal when the evacuation order came.
You duck under the table. It's large enough to hide beneath, though the legs leave you partially visible.

interactions.response: You strain against the Table. It doesn't move.
You address the Table. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Stopped Vehicle
objects.description: An alien ground transport, stopped mid-road.

then.text: A sleek ground transport — no wheels, hovering on dead repulsors an inch above the road surface. The canopy is open. Personal belongings on the passenger platform: a satchel, data crystals, what might be children's drawings on alien paper. The driver left in a hurry.
You climb into the vehicle's cargo space. It's cramped but hidden from view. The repulsors hum faintly — there's still residual power.

interactions.response: The Vehicle is firmly in place.
You mutter something at the Vehicle. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: City Map Kiosk
objects.description: A public information terminal showing a city map.

then.text: A public kiosk with a holographic city map still flickering. Districts are labeled in alien script. You can make out major landmarks by their icons — a book symbol (library), crossed weapons (war room), a gear (power station), a crystal spire (temple). The underground railway connects them all.
You tap the holographic interface. The map zooms and rotates, showing you building interiors, transit routes, and — most importantly — the path from the underground railway to the research district.

interactions.response: Moving the Kiosk would accomplish nothing.
The Kiosk has nothing to say.

objects.name: Flickering Echo
objects.description: A translucent figure materializes near the fountain.

then.text: A tall, four-armed figure shimmers into view. It's translucent, ghostly — wearing what looks like civilian clothing. It turns slowly, as if searching for someone. Its mouth moves but no sound comes. This Echo is more coherent than the ones in the wasteland.

The Echo's voice comes through the communicator, thin and distorted: "You... you're not one of us. But you're here. The library — go to the library. Our scientists left everything there. The cipher, the research, the warnings. Hurry. The crystal watcher sees all."

The stabilizer hums. The Echo solidifies slightly, enough to gesture. It points firmly toward the library district, then toward the underground. It mimes running. The message is clear: go, and go fast.
"Hello?" The Echo doesn't respond. It continues its loop — turning, searching, mouthing silent words. Without the right equipment, you can't bridge the gap.

interactions.response: You can't move the Echo.
You prod the Echo. It yields nothing useful.

objects.name: Plaza Archway
objects.description: An arched bridge connecting buildings above the plaza.

then.text: Graceful arched bridges connect the buildings surrounding the plaza, three stories up. The architecture is beautiful — sweeping curves, no sharp edges, everything flowing into everything else. Lights still glow in some of the windows above.

interactions.response: The Archway won't budge.
You fiddle with the Archway. It accomplishes nothing.
The Archway has nothing to say.

objects.name: City Spire
objects.description: One of the city's tall crystalline spires rises from the plaza's edge.

then.text: A crystalline spire rises from the plaza's edge, tapering to a point high above. Its surface is etched with geometric patterns that may be decorative or functional — perhaps both. At its base, a door-shaped panel is sealed with a keystone lock.
The keystone slots into the lock. The panel slides open silently, revealing an interior staircase spiraling upward. From above: a view of the entire city and, in the distance, the nexus.

interactions.response: You can't move the Spire.
You prod the Spire. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Spire. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Data Crystal Stacks
objects.description: Floor-to-ceiling racks of glowing data crystals.

then.text: Thousands of data crystals in precisely labeled slots, floor to ceiling. The format is identical to the Choir's archive on the ship — the Choir copied this civilization's storage technology. Or stole it. Most crystals glow faintly blue. One section glows amber — marked with a warning symbol.
You squeeze between the stacks. The rows are narrow but tall — perfect cover for someone your size. The crystals hum softly around you.

With full power restored, the crystal stacks light up completely. An automated retrieval system activates, presenting crystals to your reading station based on your searches. The library is fully operational.

interactions.response: Moving the Crystal Stacks would accomplish nothing.
The Crystal Stacks has nothing to say.

objects.name: Reading Station
objects.description: A data crystal reader with a holographic display.

then.text: A reading station with a crystal slot and a holographic projector. The projector flickers with residual power. A crystal is already loaded — someone was mid-research when the evacuation hit.

You activate the loaded crystal. A holographic display sputters to life — alien text scrolls past, accompanied by diagrams. Without the translation cipher, you can only make out a few words: 'convergence,' 'harvest,' 'weapon,' 'failure.'

With the cipher, the text becomes clear: a research report on the Convergence's energy harvesting method and the civilization's countermeasure theory. The energy can be turned back on itself — but the weapon was never fully assembled. The components were scattered across secured vaults.

interactions.response: You can't move the Reading Station.
Talking to the Reading Station yields no response.

objects.name: Holographic Index
objects.description: A library catalog system with a shimmering holographic interface.

then.text: A holographic catalog, still operational. Symbols float in the air — categories, subjects, locations. One section is highlighted in urgent red, labeled with the Convergence warning symbol. The last search query is still active: it translated roughly to 'countermeasure status.'
You navigate the index, searching for translation aids. The system presents a crystal from the linguistics section — glowing differently from the others. You pull it from the retrieval slot.
Translation Cipher Fragment 4 of 4 obtained. With all four fragments, you can assemble the complete cipher.

interactions.response: The Index won't budge.
You speak to the Index. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Convergence Research Section
objects.description: A restricted section of the library dedicated to studying the Convergence threat.

then.text: A sealed section marked with warning symbols. Through the transparent barrier you can see data crystals glowing an angry red — the civilization's research on the Convergence. A keystone lock secures the entrance.

The keystone opens the restricted section. Inside: decades of research on the Convergence. Energy patterns, planetary consumption rates, weakness analyses. And one crystal labeled in urgent script — the weapon schematics overview.
The barrier holds firm. A keystone lock requires the city's access token. This section was restricted even before the evacuation.

interactions.response: You strain against the Restricted. It doesn't move.
You address the Restricted. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Study Alcove
objects.description: A small reading alcove between the stacks.

then.text: A cozy reading alcove, built for a four-armed reader who could hold two crystals at once while taking notes with two free hands. A cushioned bench, a small reading lamp. Untouched since the evacuation.
You curl up in the alcove, pulling the cushion over you. From outside, you'd look like an oddly-shaped pillow.

interactions.response: The Alcove is firmly in place.
You mutter something at the Alcove. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Holographic Tactical Table
objects.description: A massive table projecting a 3D map of the planet.

then.text: A massive tactical table, dark. Its surface is embedded with thousands of tiny projectors. Labels around the edge — unit designations, defense grid sectors, emergency protocols. All offline. The power station could change that.

The table blazes to life. A 3D hologram of the planet rotates above it, covered in red markers — every siphon tower, every energy conduit, every harvesting node. The defense grid overlay shows orbital satellite positions, all marked OFFLINE. A controller module sits in a locked drawer beneath the table.

You pull open the drawer beneath the table. Inside: the defense grid controller — the interface for the orbital satellite network. With enough power, this could reactivate the planet's last line of defense.
Dead. The table needs external power. The city's power station might still be restorable.

interactions.response: Moving the Tactical Table would accomplish nothing.
The Tactical Table has nothing to say.

objects.name: Tactical Displays
objects.description: Wall-mounted screens showing battle plans.

then.text: Tactical screens on the walls, some still dimly lit by backup power. Battle formations, retreat routes, civilian evacuation plans. The final entries show a desperate assault plan — a strike team heading into the Convergence nexus itself. The team's route is marked: through the underground railway, under the city, into the crystal heart. They never came back.

interactions.response: You can't move the Displays.
You prod the Displays. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Displays. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Communications Array
objects.description: Military communication equipment, some still powered.

then.text: Military-grade communication equipment. Most channels are dead, but the backup power feeds a few receivers. Static hisses from speakers. The last logged transmission, timestamped to the final day: 'Strike team has entered the nexus. All units fall back to evacuation points. May the resonance carry us home.'

You scan through frequencies. Dead. Dead. Static. Dead. Then — a faint rhythmic pulse. Not a voice. Not a signal. A heartbeat. The Convergence's energy has a rhythm, and it's broadcasting on every frequency.

interactions.response: Moving the Comms would accomplish nothing.
The Comms has nothing to say.

objects.name: Battle Plans
objects.description: Printed tactical documents spread across a secondary table.

then.text: With the cipher, the battle plans reveal everything: the nexus assault route, the weapon assembly location inside the nexus, the escape shaft the team carved as a fallback. They knew exactly what they were doing. They just didn't have enough time to finish the weapon.

Physical documents — alien paper with dense tactical writing and diagrams. You can make out the nexus structure in cross-section, arrows showing an assault path, and what looks like a weapon schematic. Without the translation cipher, the details are lost.

interactions.response: You can't move the Plans.
You prod the Plans. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Plans. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Equipment Locker
objects.description: A military storage locker, partially open.

then.text: A military equipment locker, door hanging open. Most contents were taken during the evacuation — empty weapon racks, cleared shelves. But a few items remain: emergency rations (long expired), a damaged comm device, and a personal locket wedged behind a shelf.
You squeeze inside the locker. It's dark and cramped but provides good cover.

interactions.response: Moving the Locker would accomplish nothing.
The Locker has nothing to say.

objects.name: Commander's Chair
objects.description: A large chair at the head of the tactical table.

then.text: A command chair, designed for a four-armed occupant. The armrests are worn smooth from years of use. Whoever sat here made the hardest decisions of the war. On the seat: a folded cloth — a personal standard or flag, left behind when the last commander vacated.

interactions.response: You can't move the Chair.
You prod the Chair. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Chair. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Prototype Weapon
objects.description: An incomplete energy weapon on a central platform.

then.text: A partially assembled energy weapon on a containment platform. Crystalline components fused with metal framework. It's elegant — designed to channel and redirect Convergence energy back at its source. But key components are missing: the core, the dampener, the focusing crystal. The assembly was abandoned mid-work.
The prototype is fused to its platform — it can't be moved. But studying it gives you insight into how the components fit together. This is a reference model, not the weapon itself.

interactions.response: Moving the Prototype would accomplish nothing.
The Prototype has nothing to say.

objects.name: Research Workstation
objects.description: A scientist's workstation with active holographic schematics.

then.text: A research workstation, holographic displays still active on minimal power. Weapon schematics hover in the air — detailed cross-sections of the countermeasure device. Notes in alien script surround the diagrams.

With the cipher, the schematics become clear: assembly instructions for the countermeasure. Weapon core seats into the resonance crystal housing. Energy dampener wraps the assembly. Siphon crystal fragment provides the ignition charge. You memorize the sequence.
You study the holographic displays but can't read the annotations. The diagrams alone show component shapes and positions, but without translation you're guessing at the assembly order.

interactions.response: You can't move the Workstation.
Talking to the Workstation yields no response.

objects.name: Weapon Schematics
objects.description: Detailed holographic schematics of the countermeasure device.

then.text: Floating holographic weapon schematics. The design is elegant: a three-component device that captures, reverses, and amplifies the Convergence's own energy. The theory is sound — the execution was what failed. They ran out of time.
You can't take a hologram. But the workstation has a portable data crystal reader — you download the schematics to a blank crystal.

interactions.response: The Schematics won't budge.
You fiddle with the Schematics. It accomplishes nothing.
The Schematics has nothing to say.

objects.name: Energy Containment Field
objects.description: A shimmering field containing raw Convergence energy samples.

then.text: A containment field holding samples of raw Convergence energy. The energy pulses and writhes inside the field like a living thing. This is what the scientists were studying — the enemy's blood, captured and contained.
You reach toward the field and snatch your hand back — the air around it burns with static electricity. The field is holding but deteriorating. Touching it unprotected would be lethal.

interactions.response: You can't move the Containment.
Talking to the Containment yields no response.

objects.name: Equipment Rack
objects.description: Scientific instruments and protective equipment.

then.text: Racks of scientific equipment: energy meters, calibration tools, safety equipment. Most are sized for four-armed users, but a pair of goggles and some smaller instruments might work for you.
You take a pair of safety goggles. They're oversized but adjustable — you tighten the strap to fit. These should protect against energy flashes in the nexus.

interactions.response: The Equipment won't budge.
You fiddle with the Equipment. It accomplishes nothing.
The Equipment has nothing to say.

objects.name: Supply Cabinet
objects.description: A tall cabinet with lab supplies.

then.text: A tall supply cabinet with sliding doors. Large enough to hide inside, with ventilation slits that would let you see out.
You slide open the cabinet and climb inside, pulling the door almost shut behind you. Through the ventilation slits, you can watch the lab without being seen.

interactions.response: You can't move the Cabinet.
Talking to the Cabinet yields no response.

objects.name: Open Doorway
objects.description: An open doorway into an alien home.

then.text: An open doorway into someone's home. Inside: curved furniture designed for four-armed beings, a low table with an unfinished game, artwork on the walls showing landscapes that no longer exist. It's heartbreakingly ordinary. Someone lived here. Loved here. Left everything behind.
You slip inside the home and crouch behind the curved sofa. The furniture is oversized for you — perfect cover. Through the window you can watch the street.

interactions.response: The Doorway won't budge.
You speak to the Doorway. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Children's Toys
objects.description: Alien toys scattered on the floor of a home.

then.text: Toys scattered on the floor. Four-armed action figures. Building blocks with alien geometry. A stuffed creature that might be this world's equivalent of a teddy bear. A child was playing here when the evacuation was called. The toys are still warm — not literally, but they hold the warmth of normalcy. This is the hardest thing you've seen yet.

interactions.response: You strain against the Toys. It doesn't move.
You touch the Toys. Nothing happens.
Talking to the Toys yields no response.

objects.name: Packed Luggage
objects.description: Hastily packed bags left in a doorway.

then.text: Bags packed in a hurry — clothes spilling out, a data crystal reader shoved in sideways, alien identification documents. They were planning to evacuate. They packed. They never left.

You search through the luggage. Personal effects, clothing sized for four-armed beings, preserved food packets (long expired). Nothing useful... wait. Tucked in a side pocket: a small personal locket, the kind worn around the neck.

interactions.response: The Luggage won't budge.
You speak to the Luggage. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Family Portraits
objects.description: A wall of alien family photographs.

then.text: Family portraits on the wall. The alien equivalent of photographs — holographic captures frozen in crystal frames. A family of four — two adults, two children. All four-armed, all smiling in their alien way. The children are playing. The adults watch with what can only be love. This species was not so different from yours.

interactions.response: You strain against the Portraits. It doesn't move.
You touch the Portraits. Nothing happens.
Talking to the Portraits yields no response.

objects.name: Residential Echo
objects.description: A ghostly figure appears in the doorway of a home.

then.text: An Echo — a tall figure in a doorway, looking back into a home that no longer exists as they remember it. This one is more coherent than most. Their four arms hang at their sides. Their face shows something universal: grief.

You hold up the locket. The Echo SEES it. Its form solidifies, its expression shifting from grief to recognition. Through the communicator: "That was... mine. My family. I couldn't... we couldn't get out in time. The children..." A long silence. "The temple. Go to the temple. The prophecy speaks of one who comes after. That's you. Take the prophet's crystal. It will show you the way."
Through the communicator: "Who are you? You're so small. Are you... from the specimens? They took you too? I'm sorry. I'm so sorry for everything." The Echo flickers. It's losing coherence.
You speak softly. The Echo doesn't respond — it can't hear you without the right equipment. It continues its silent vigil in the doorway.

interactions.response: The Echo won't budge.
You fiddle with the Echo. It accomplishes nothing.

objects.name: Abandoned Meal
objects.description: A meal for one, left on a kitchen counter.

then.text: A single serving of alien food on a counter. The food has petrified into grey stone. A beverage glass, half-empty. Someone was eating alone when the world ended. They didn't even finish their drink.

interactions.response: You strain against the Meal. It doesn't move.
You touch the Meal. Nothing happens.
Talking to the Meal yields no response.

objects.name: Reactor Chamber
objects.description: The city's main power reactor, partially operational.

then.text: The city's main reactor — a large cylindrical chamber with energy cores that glow faintly. It's on standby power: enough for emergency systems but not the full grid. The engineering is impressive — robust, built to last millennia. And it has, mostly.

Too high to reach. The reactor controls are at full-height alien console level. But the adapter bridges technologies — you connect it to a low-level maintenance port and route power from the adapter's reserves to jump-start the reactor.

interactions.response: The Reactor won't budge.
You speak to the Reactor. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Power Distribution Panel
objects.description: Controls for routing power to different city districts.

then.text: A power distribution panel — toggle switches for each city district. Currently all offline. Labels identify each district: library, temple, war room, research, residential, railway, and — ominously — 'deep transit' leading down toward the nexus.

With the reactor running, the panel comes alive. But the gauges show limited power — you can only activate 3 of 7 districts. Choose carefully: each district you power up reveals new interactions and resources, but also makes that area visible to The Watcher.
Dead switches. Without the reactor running, there's nothing to distribute.

interactions.response: You strain against the Power Panel. It doesn't move.
You address the Power Panel. Predictably, silence.

objects.name: Backup Systems
objects.description: Emergency backup power units along the wall.

then.text: Emergency backup units — these are what's been keeping the city's minimal systems running for millennia. Status indicators show most at 2-5% capacity. One unit is at 15% — relatively fresh. A power cell adapter port is visible on each unit.
You find a universal power cell adapter mounted on the side of the freshest backup unit. This bridges alien and human technology — it could interface with anything.

interactions.response: The Backup is firmly in place.
You mutter something at the Backup. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Convergence Breach
objects.description: Crystalline growths pushing through the station wall.

then.text: Crystalline Convergence growths have breached the station wall, pushing through concrete and metal like roots through soil. The crystals pulse with stolen energy. This is how the Convergence spreads — it literally grows through infrastructure, consuming and converting.
The crystals are razor-sharp and thrumming with energy. Touching them would be extremely dangerous. But they're warm — warm with the stolen life of a planet.

interactions.response: Moving the Breach would accomplish nothing.
The Breach has nothing to say.

objects.name: Power Conduits
objects.description: Thick energy conduits running between the reactor and the distribution panel.

then.text: Heavy power conduits connecting the reactor to the distribution panel. They're dark now, but you can see where they branch off to feed each city district. Robust engineering — minimal damage despite millennia of neglect.

interactions.response: You can't move the Conduits.
You prod the Conduits. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Conduits. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Maintenance Hatch
objects.description: A floor-level maintenance hatch.

then.text: A floor-level maintenance hatch. It's sized for maintenance drones, not full-sized workers — but it's perfect for someone your size. Leads to the conduit tunnels beneath the station.
You pull the hatch open and drop into the narrow maintenance tunnel beneath. It's cramped but completely hidden from above.

interactions.response: Moving the Hatch would accomplish nothing.
The Hatch has nothing to say.

objects.name: Resonance Chamber
objects.description: A circular depression in the temple floor that glows with energy.

then.text: A circular depression in the floor, lined with crystalline material that glows faintly. This is where the inhabitants communed through vibration — a species that spoke through subsonic resonance, like the Choir but natural. The chamber still resonates when you step near it.

You strike the tuning fork and hold it over the chamber. The crystal lining SINGS — a deep, beautiful tone that fills the temple. Echoes manifest around you, dozens of them, a congregation of the dead. For one moment, the temple is alive again. Then the resonance fades, and they fade with it. But the chamber's energy has unlocked something at the altar.

You step into the chamber. The crystal hums around you, responding to your presence. Faint vibrations travel through your bones. But without the right frequency, you can't activate the full resonance.

interactions.response: You can't move the Resonance Chamber.
Talking to the Resonance Chamber yields no response.

objects.name: Temple Altar
objects.description: A stone altar with alien offerings.

then.text: A stone altar with offerings: dried alien flowers, crystalline tokens, small figurines of the four-armed species. A sealed compartment in the altar's base bears the temple's resonance symbol. Above it, an inscription you can barely make out.

The resonance has unsealed the altar compartment. Inside: a crystal unlike any you've seen — perfectly clear, with swirling patterns of light inside that seem to show... images. Possible futures. The prophet's crystal.
The altar compartment is sealed — the resonance lock holds firm. The temple's resonance chamber might hold the key.
Among the offerings, you find a resonance tuning fork — a crystalline instrument used in the species' meditation practices. It hums when you touch it.

interactions.response: The Altar won't budge.
You speak to the Altar. Your words fall flat.

objects.name: Temple Murals
objects.description: Wall paintings depicting the species' history and prophecy.

then.text: Murals covering the walls, painted in pigments that still glow after millennia. They tell a story: the species rising from simple beginnings, building cities, reaching the stars. A golden age. Then darkness — a crystalline force arriving from deep space. The final panels show a small figure — tiny compared to the four-armed inhabitants — standing before a great crystal. The prophecy of 'the one who comes after.'

With the cipher, the inscriptions beneath each mural become clear. The prophecy reads: 'When the crystal consumes the last light, one will come from the specimens. Small of body, vast of will. They will carry what we could not finish. They will face the heart of the crystal. They will choose.' The murals show six possible endings — six paths the 'small one' might take. Some end in light. Some in darkness. All end in choice.

interactions.response: You strain against the Murals. It doesn't move.
You touch the Murals. Nothing happens.
Talking to the Murals yields no response.

objects.name: Offerings
objects.description: Small offerings left by worshippers.

then.text: Small personal offerings: crystalline tokens, tiny figurines, pressed alien flowers. Each one represents a prayer, a hope, a farewell. The last offerings were desperate — hastily placed, some still clutched by ghost-hands that have long since faded.

interactions.response: The Offerings won't budge.
You fiddle with the Offerings. It accomplishes nothing.
The Offerings has nothing to say.

objects.name: Crystal Walls
objects.description: The temple's crystalline walls filter light beautifully.

then.text: The temple walls are grown from living crystal — or were, once. The crystal is dead now, but it still filters light beautifully, casting prismatic patterns across the floor. The craftsmanship is stunning — this species built with crystal the way humans build with glass.

interactions.response: You can't move the Crystal Walls.
You prod the Crystal Walls. It yields nothing useful.
You mutter something at the Crystal Walls. It doesn't answer.

objects.name: Meditation Alcove
objects.description: A small alcove for private meditation.

then.text: A small alcove for private meditation, with a cushioned seat and a crystal resonance panel on the back wall. Intimate, quiet, sheltered from view.
You slip into the alcove and pull the crystal curtain across. In the dim crystalline light, you're nearly invisible.
